articles.title: Recapping the recent Pokemon TCG PH Controversy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The recent controversy surrounding the Pokemon TCG community has renewed conversation on safe spaces. You’re walking around an event, happy to see your hobby out in full…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The recent controversy surrounding the Pokemon TCG community has renewed conversation on safe spaces.

You’re walking around an event, happy to see your hobby out in full display. With how frequently hobby gatherings and events have been happening, it’s no surprise that these interests would eventually be monetized one way or another. Communities form, guards come down, and a sense of familiarity takes over.

You’d think the hobby space was safe, seeing the same vendors over and over again across a variety of events. But what happens when that familiarity is challenged? All the trust and goodwill established over months, possibly even years, can come crashing down when allegations of inappropriate behavior involving a familiar vendor come to light.
What happened in the Filipino Pokemon TCG space?

Recently, an ongoing controversy involving seller Jaime “TipsyJ” Tolentino began circulating on the Pokémon TCG Philippines subreddit, originating from a thread warning the community about his alleged predatory behavior.

The discussion stemmed from leaked group chat messages that reportedly showed multiple instances of inappropriate conduct, including alleged gestures toward a woman wearing shorts and inappropriate attention toward a minor wearing a Gengar jacket.
Another member of the group chat, “1MPIRE”, was also criticized for allegedly objectifying women in his immediate vicinity.

Following the circulation of these messages, local event organizer MNL Card Convention removed TipsyJ as a vendor and sponsor from its event. As more individuals began speaking out about the allegations, others came to his defense.

However, members of the community questioned these defenses, noting the apparent connections between the individuals involved and the same vendor circle. Several members of that circle subsequently faced criticism and calls for boycotts over their alleged involvement or enabling behavior.

With discussions about TipsyJ spreading across Reddit and Facebook, another vendor and then moderator of the Facebook group Pokemon Collectors Group PH Buy & Sell 🇵🇭 (TCG & More), “Tondo Cartel”, also became involved in the controversy after allegedly seeking ways to trace the IP addresses of anonymous Reddit users.
As updates continued to circulate, the situation eventually caught the attention of international TCG content creators.
What might otherwise have remained a localized hobby controversy reached an international audience when American TCG content creator and patent attorney “UMU” took notice of the situation.
After sharing a screenshot of a Reddit thread featuring an apology from “Tondo Cartel” that drew criticism from community members, the vendor subsequently threatened legal action against “UMU.”

Following allegations of attempts to identify anonymous users, discussions about Reddit IP tracing, and legal threats against individuals commenting on the controversy, both “Tondo Cartel” and TipsyJ eventually issued apologies.
Despite this, members of the community continued to call for accountability, with questions remaining about the conduct of those involved and how the situation was handled.
RELATED STORY: Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek full set review
Making a living out of a hobby
The hobby space is filled with opportunities for monetization, with content creators and resellers being just a small part of an economic ecosystem that helps drive its growth.
With Pokémon being the franchise that it is, there’s no doubt that people across different age groups and backgrounds would find something to appreciate, making it a community with a diverse fanbase.

As interest grows, financial opportunities naturally follow, turning something that was once purely recreational into a potential business. In the collectibles space, for example, randomly collecting items growing up would bring a certain excitement whenever you found something that aligned with your interests. However, the dynamic changes when money gets involved.

That collectible you once had multiples of growing up could eventually become a retro commodity with its own market value. What starts as an opportunity to sell a few items can eventually turn into something bigger.

As capital grows with each sale and childhood collections are gradually liquidated, the doors to running an entire buy-and-sell business open up. It gets even more involved once importing products and establishing supplier relationships enter the picture, taking things further away from simply being a hobby.

Of course, turning a hobby into a business isn’t always the end goal. Plenty of individuals remain in their respective communities simply because they enjoy collecting, playing, or meeting people who share their interests.
However, the growing commercial side of these hobbies can also make it increasingly difficult for newcomers to participate.

Pokémon, for example, has been around for three decades and continues to enjoy widespread recognition. Yet with scalping, rising collectible prices, and other market factors, getting younger players into the physical trading card game can be a challenge.

While mobile alternatives such as Pokémon TCG Pocket provide another way to experience the franchise, there’s still something meaningful about owning and playing with physical cards featuring your favorite Pokémon.
There’s nothing inherently wrong with collectibles maintaining their value, nor is there anything wrong with people making a living out of their interests.

However, when the cost of participating becomes a barrier for younger audiences, it raises questions about accessibility and the future of the hobby. After all, children are among the very audiences that Pokémon continues to appeal to, and keeping the game accessible to them should remain part of the conversation.
Maintaining a safe space in the hobby scene
The TCG space has always had its share of bad actors, but seeing allegations of this nature emerge within a hobby that attracts younger audiences is particularly disappointing.

Beyond the accusations involving TipsyJ, the controversy also raises questions about the applicability of Republic Act No. 11313, or the Safe Spaces Act, particularly its provisions concerning gender-based sexual harassment in public spaces and online. Determining whether specific acts constitute violations of the law, however, would require further investigation.
Despite the controversy, the community response does offer some hope. Seeing individuals speak out, question questionable behavior, and demand accountability is something worth commending.

However, identifying bad actors and addressing misconduct should not fall solely on community members. Event organizers and vendors also have a responsibility to establish standards of conduct, particularly when their events attract younger audiences.
While the Philippine TCG events scene continues to grow, maintaining a welcoming environment should be just as important as expanding its commercial opportunities.

Organizers should have accessible channels for reporting misconduct, vendors should be held to consistent standards, and individuals who raise legitimate concerns should not have to worry about intimidation or retaliation.

There may be legitimate sellers who find themselves caught in the crossfire, but that shouldn’t discourage the community from asking questions and exercising caution. Supporting your local game store, attending events, and trying out the game should remain enjoyable experiences rather than something people have to approach with apprehension.

Sometimes, the magic is in the gathering, and the monetary aspect becomes less important. It’s having that safe space that makes hobbies enjoyable, especially when you’re surrounded by people who share the same passion and enthusiasm.

Not everyone could catch them all, but if there’s anything worth celebrating about this controversy, it’s seeing a community band together to protect the very thing that brought them together in the first place.

articles.title: Bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant, prompting evacuations
articles.summary:
Peoria officials said a bomb was found at BioUrja Renewables and later defused; FBI said it is investigating

Residents were ordered to evacuate parts of an

blocks.text: Residents were ordered to evacuate parts of an Illinois community on Friday after the mayor there said authorities found a bomb at a local ethanol- and alcohol-production plant.

The discovery reported at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria triggered a mandatory evacuation over a one-mile evacuation zone encompassing sections of that city as well as the adjacent municipality of East Peoria.
“It is real – this is a real thing,” Peoria’s mayor, Rita Ali, said, according to local news outlet WMBD. “We know that is a real threat. We know it is a bomb.”
Peoria’s police chief, Brad Dixon, said at a news conference early on Saturday that bomb technicians had rendered the object in question safe.
But Dixon asked for the public’s patience as investigators searched BioUrja Renewals’ expansive facility for other explosive devices, as the Peoria news outlet WEEK reported.
“We don’t know if there are other devices,” Ali remarked.

Meanwhile, Ryan Presley of the FBI, who is in charge of the bureau’s field office about an hour away in Springfield, Illinois, said agents would pursue whoever was responsible “tirelessly” and “bring them to justice”.

At about 7.05pm local time on Friday, the Peoria police department had announced that officers were “actively investigating a reported bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables”. The agency then urged “anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to immediately evacuate their homes and businesses until further notice”.

The police’s statement said the evacuation notice had been “issued out of an abundance of caution while officers and emergency personnel investigate the threat”, which officials initially referred to as a suspicious package. The city offered the Manual Academy school as a temporary shelter, and police said anyone who needed assistance evacuating their home or business could call for help.

In a separate statement, the municipal government of neighboring East Peoria acknowledged that the evacuation zone associated with the package at BioUrja Renewables extended into part of that city. The East Peoria government said it expected to provide an update at about 9am local time on Saturday, but in the meantime all evacuations would remain in place.
“This is not a hoax,” the Illinois state senator Dave Koehler said during the early Saturday news conference. “This has gone beyond that … This is serious. This is serious.”

Friday’s BioUrja Renewables case came amid a particularly chaotic day in the US marked by a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration-ordered nationwide ground stop at US airports that was in effect for about four hours, canceling or delaying more than 11,000 US flights.

The country’s nerves were also frayed by a tanker which struck a cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon. First responders had to rescue passengers from the river’s water after the cruise ship turned on its side, and there were more than 30 injuries reported. But none of those injuries were critical, and there were no fatalities reported in association with the crash.

articles.title: DFA: 80% of South China Sea Code of Conduct completed, salient issues remain
articles.summary: Southeast Asian nations and China have completed negotiations on 80% of the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) on the South China Sea ahead of next week's ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Department of…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 10:11pm

Southeast Asian nations and China have completed negotiations on 80% of the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) on the South China Sea ahead of next week's ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Saturday.
At a news conference in Pasay City, DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said significant progress had been made in the COC negotiations under the Philippines' ASEAN chairship.

"Since our chairship, a lot has been, the progress of the Code of Conduct is really hastened and there might just be a definitive possibility, but definitely a statement will be released," Lazaro said.

"Let's give it a little bit more time, as this is still subject of discussions. But I just want to say, at this point of time, 80% of the paragraphs, the paper itself, the document itself is finished. So, there will be just some salient points," she added.

The proposed code seeks to establish rules to prevent disputes in the South China Sea from spiraling out of control and developing into a major armed conflict that could involve the United States, a Philippine ally, and other countries in the region.

Lazaro earlier said ASEAN and China want to avoid a situation in the South China Sea similar to that in the Strait of Hormuz, which has prompted both sides to pursue negotiations on a Code of Conduct.
Malacañang, meanwhile, said it remains hopeful that the COC will be signed before the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship ends.
"Bawat araw dapat may pag-asa (Every day should bring hope)," Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.

"Sa ngayon, hindi rin natin masasabi kung talagang hindi ito magkakaroon ng konklusyon sa 49th ASEAN Summit dahil ang gusto pa rin ng Pangulo ay masapinal sa panahon na ang Pilipinas ang ASEAN chair," she added.
(At this point, we cannot say for certain that the issue will not be resolved during the 49th ASEAN Summit, as the President still wants it finalized while the Philippines holds the ASEAN chairship.)

Four ASEAN member states—Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, and Brunei—are involved in the long-standing territorial disputes in the South China Sea, an important passageway for global trade and commerce. The other two claimants are China and Taiwan.

In August 2018, ASEAN and China agreed on a single draft of the COC. In November 2018, both sides agreed to finalize the document within three years, beginning in 2019. However, no final agreement has been reached since then. —VBL, GMA News

The UK should have a milder weekend as the unusual autumn freeze eases off, after…

blocks.text: The UK should have a milder weekend as the unusual autumn freeze eases off, after cold health alerts were issued and temperatures plummeted overnight, forecasters have said.

After frost on Saturday morning, most of the UK should enjoy a “fine day with some sunshine”, the Met Office said. However, it will not be blue skies for everyone, as torrential rain and showers are predicted to move in from the west, bringing patchy rain and strong winds across the north and far west of the UK.
Snow is also on the cards for north-west Scotland, the Met Office said. Temperatures on Saturday morning were expected to vary between 5C (41F) in Norwich and Manchester and 11C in Plymouth

The mild reprieve will be welcome to many Britons after temperatures on Friday night fell as low as -6.6C in Sennybridge, near Bannau Brycheiniog in south Wales, and -6.5C in Shap, a village near Penrith in Cumbria.
The first yellow cold health alerts of the season were issued this week by the UK Health Security Agency for the West Midlands and the north-west, and remained in place until midday on Saturday.

These alerts indicated the weather was “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life to vulnerable people, the agency said.

blocks.caption: A dog walker braves a cold and frosty morning in the Oxfordshire countryside. Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Eastern parts of England should have drier spells on Saturday evening, with clear spells and some frost. But other parts of the UK would be cloudy, with passing showers, the forecaster said.

On Sunday, temperatures are expected to stay above freezing in the morning. Sunshine is expected to brighten things up in the east, and the UK’s far north and west will also be treated to a bit of sunshine later in the day.

articles.title: Trump ‘whiplash’ on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: ‘People already survived a war’
articles.summary:
Members of Congress and advocates warn that returning people to their home countries could be a death sentence

Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to…

blocks.text: Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days.
Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence.

A flight originally scheduled to transport the group out of the US on election day earlier this month had stayed grounded after a federal judge issued a court order temporarily blocking its departure to Afghanistan or neighboring Pakistan. The whole group numbers more than 150 Afghans, the New York Times reported. And the AP previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

blocks.caption: Afghan refugees arrive at a deportation center in Landi Kotal near the Torkham border crossing in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on 28 April. Photograph: Abdul Majeed/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Then, as the temporary court order expired last weekend, immigration advocates battling to prevent the deportations talked of dreading that the detainees could be forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November . This prospect was based on a rescheduled removal date given for at least one Afghan man currently in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention who was due to be on the flight.
As that date loomed, suddenly there was another development amid frantic advocacy efforts.

Late on Tuesday, it was learned that that detainee, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, now no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government.

Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they would not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days after all.

Amid some confusion and often few details from the administration, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the US non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, said that a sensation of “fragile relief” had descended on the people involved.

Some of the Afghans in the targeted group have relatives who assisted the US war on Afghanistan after the terrorist attacks on the US on 11 September 2001 that drove out the Taliban, VanDiver said. He had already called Donald Trump’s efforts to remove Afghans from the US cruel and being done in “a heinous matter” as a scare tactic against others.

“In a matter of days, these allies were told they were being sent through Pakistan into the hands of the Taliban, then told they were safe, then told that nobody knows. That isn’t immigration policy. It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said. “These men and women kept their promise to America, and it’s time we kept ours by ending these removals for good.”
VanDiver has slammed any option to use Pakistan as a conduit for “forced rendition”.

Immigration advocates are hoping continued pressure will result in further delays and the ultimate cancellation of that flight and any others planned for the coming weeks. In the meantime, #AfghanEvac is pushing what will become the newly Democratic-controlled Congress in January to pass a bipartisan bill that has been drafted and would give Afghans who are already in the US temporary protected status (TPS) through July 2029, with a vetting process. The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans.

blocks.caption: An Afghan national and her son in the National Conference Center in Leesburg, Virginia, which was redesigned to temporarily house Afghan nationals, on 11 August 2022. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

blocks.text: Such legislation would “keep people we already vetted and brought here from being sent back to the Taliban while their cases are decided”, VanDiver said.

Among the passengers reported to be on the blocked flight were Afghans whose relatives helped American troops, women, at least one gay man and members of the minority ethnic Hazara group – some who have said they were previously beaten by the Taliban.

Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “grave, systematic dangers” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan. That includes “arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence”, as well as restrictions on basic freedoms for women and girls.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to questions and a request for comment that the agency complies with all lawful court orders and that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) does not comment on or confirm prospective removal operations, for operational security reasons, and the safety of its officers.

Sari Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the Trump administration’s targeting of Afghans reflects a broader trend of creating arrangements with other governments to send people back to war zones, security crises and countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with the US.
The US suspended relations with Afghanistan after the Taliban government took over in 2021, forcing a scrambled US evacuation.

blocks.caption: Taliban fighters celebrate after the US pulled out of the country, in Kabul on 31 August 2021. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Trump administration has held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians via a third country, and last Sunday an attorney reported that the US deportation flight of Iranian nationals headed to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled, according to the AP.

The Trump administration also is increasingly deporting immigrants to such “third countries”. The supreme court is still litigating in what circumstances the federal government can deport people to regions they have no connection to, though in late September, the court ruled on an emergency basis, allowing Trump to continue this practice.
Federal law is designed to prevent the US government from forcing someone to return to a country where they are likely to face torture.

The DHS said in a statement that immigrants sent to a third country “receive notice and an opportunity to challenge their removal unless the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries” that they would be safe upon return.

More than 60 concerned lawmakers in Congress signed a letter to the DHS and the state department, citing relevant law and also calling for the cancellation of any deportation flights of Afghans or Iranians to their home countries, either directly or through any other country. “The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way,” the letter stated.

In another letter, New York congressman Gregory Meeks and US senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, both Democrats, wrote to Pakistan’s ambassador to the US, urging the Pakistani government not to collaborate in any operation to fly Afghans to Pakistan and then expel them over the border to Afghanistan. The Pakistani embassy did not respond to a request for comment.

blocks.caption: A celebration to mark the fifth anniversary of the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan, in Kabul on 15 August. Photograph: Samiullah Popal/EPA

blocks.text: The Afghans targeted are believed to have final removal orders, which means the US can legally deport them. But the fact that an immigrant failed to get asylum or prove to the Trump administration that they have a credible fear about returning to their home country does not mean they don’t face serious risks in their native country, critics argue.

The US state department advises Americans: “Do not travel to Afghanistan for any reason,” warning of “civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities”. The risks for returning Afghans are seen as much greater.

“We are talking about people who’ve already been tortured, people who came with evidence – some of the most compelling claims – and the idea that they could find themselves on this flight is pretty horrifying,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. “Why would we send Iranians to a war zone or Afghans to one of the most repressive regimes in the world knowing, indeed, that they are going to be targeted because of the very vulnerabilities that led them to flee in the first place?”

One Afghan national expected to be on any deportation flight, who has been detained in ICE custody since late 2024, fears returning because his wife is a former member of Afghanistan’s military before the Taliban took over, according to court documents. He is also part of the Hazara Shia group and said he has previously been severely beaten by the Taliban while they searched for his wife.

blocks.caption: Afghan refugees, fleeing the capital Kabul, exit a US Air Force plane upon their arrival at Pristina international airport near Pristina, Kosovo, on 29 August 2021. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Shaw Drake, assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law and co-counsel for the man, said the immigration judge’s not being swayed by these risk factors was “absolutely absurd”. Drake argues that his client had no notice or opportunity to present a claim of fear of persecution or torture in Pakistan.

The man’s mental health deteriorated when he was transferred to detention in El Paso, Texas, so much so that a federal court in New Mexico issued a stay for 14 days to ensure the government had enacted safeguards to protect him from the risk of suicide.

Another Afghan who could be put on a flight is a Hazara man who testified to immigration officials that he worried about being killed by the Taliban because he reported them to the police when they killed his father, according to US government documents. He said that a few years ago, he was captured, detained, tortured and threatened with death by the Taliban, whose members electrocuted him and beat him with sticks. US federal asylum officers acknowledged the detainee’s testimony but concluded there was insufficient evidence to show the Taliban would inflict severe mental or physical harm towards him if he were sent back.

Madhavi Narayanan, a lawyer at Human Rights First, who represents him, said: “It’s another confirmation that our immigration system is not equipped to help those who are fleeing persecution and genuinely seeking safety.”

articles.summary:
Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter

When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a…

blocks.text: When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio, the company had only one option: shut the mine down for good.

For locals in and around Fairport Harbor, it means the loss of 77 jobs; but for the wider region, which depends on its salt reserves to keep roads ice- and snow-free every winter, it could mean travel chaos.

On top of that, in the weeks since the mine’s closure what’s been concerning mining experts and residents alike across the Great Lakes region is the mine’s location – about 2,000ft (610 meters) underneath Lake Erie. And that is sending broader warning signals across the region among activists and environmentalists, as to whether the issue could eventually hit other mines underneath the Great Lakes.
At the Fairport Harbor facility, one of 12 rock salt mines that Morton Salt runs around the world, around 1.3 million tons of rock salt were mined from underneath the lake every year.
Last winter’s colder and snowier than average weather ate into road salt stockpiles at hundreds of municipalities across the region.
Situated 30 miles (48km) from the now-shuttered mine, Trumbull county’s 200,000 residents relied entirely on the Fairport Harbor mine for road salt.
Trumbull county’s location downwind of Lake Erie means its roads and highways are particularly affected by lake-effect snowstorms and the freeze-thaw process for up to five months a year.
“We get about 30,000 tons [of salt] a year from the mine. But we have a stockpile of around 14,000 tons,” says David DeChristofaro, the Trumbull county engineer.

“We are waiting for the Ohio department of transportation [to see about acquiring additional road salt supplies]. If necessary, we will mix salt with aggregate, one to one, as was typically done 15 years ago, to stretch our supply of salt. But that adds to cost because it needs to be swept up at the end of winter.” Trumbull county gets around 4.5ft (1.4 meters) of snowfall every winter.
Authorities in a township in a neighboring county have had to issue a warning to motorists about potentially hazardous driving conditions this winter because of the salt shortage.

While the mine closure could mean transportation problems for more than a million residents in a region of Ohio that experiences especially harsh winter conditions, the water intrusion has also raised safety questions.

With five salt mines situated partly or entirely underneath Great Lakes waterways – in Fairport Harbor, Detroit and Cleveland, and two over the Canadian border in Ontario – a growing concern is that weeks later, Morton Salt officials say they still can’t find the source of the water intrusion.

The salt is extracted by drilling and using explosives, and while the distance between the bed of Lake Erie and Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine is in excess of 1,000ft (305 meters), decades of blasting and the presence of underground aquifers could contribute to significant subterranean rock movement, say experts.

“Blasting can fracture rock near an excavation, and removing rock changes the stresses carried by the roof, pillars and surrounding layers. For water to enter, there must also be a connected pathway from a water source to the mine,” says Xiong “Bill” Yu, a professor of engineering at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

“A nearby aquifer could supply that water through a fault, connected fractures, or a compromised shaft or seal. More than 1,000ft of rock is meaningful separation, but the engineering question is whether the layers provide a continuous barrier and whether anything crosses it.”

While the likelihood that the lake is the source of the water entering the Morton salt mine appears to be remote, local voices have begun calling for an investigation into just how safe salt mines carved out from under large bodies of water are and whether drinking water resources may be affected.

“Could the rock roof be breached, creating saline water swamps in a Lake Erie that’s the source of drinking water for millions in both the US and Canada?” an editorial in the Cleveland Plain Dealer asked this month.
after newsletter promotion

In 2017, the much larger Cargill-run Whiskey Island salt mine 30 miles (48km) west of Fairport Harbor experienced a water intrusion event that also saw dangerous levels of hydrogen sulfide gas released. That facility, which is one of the largest of its kind in the world, producing up to 4m tons a year and supplying road salt for states across the Great Lakes and midwest, spreads out 16 sq miles (41 sq km) beneath Lake Erie. More than 200 employees work 12-hour shifts there every day.

In 1994, one of the largest salt mines in the world, located in western New York, was inundated with aquifer water and collapsed. And in 1980, Lake Peigneur in Louisiana was accidentally drained when an oil rig breached the roof of an underwater salt mine 1,300ft (396 moeters) under the surface of the lake. No salt miners were injured in either incident.

The Mine Safety and Health Administration, a federal agency, oversees health and safety operations in US mines. But under the Trump administration, a deregulation drive has been enacted that includes, among other measures, eliminating diesel particle matter exposure levels in mines.

In 2022, under the Biden administration, a Morton Salt mine in Louisiana was placed on the Department of Labor’s pattern-of-violations notice for “a high number of significant and substantial violations and other safety and health compliance problems”. That notice was lifted in April 2025.

Emails sent and calls made by the Guardian to Morton Salt asking how often the Fairport Harbor mine underwent a full perimeter inspection for water intrusion before its closure, whether the company knows the source of the water intrusion, and if it is scheduling any new or improved safety measures at other mines it operates were not responded to.

Emails sent to Cargill inquiring about any potential additional safety steps it may be taking at its Whiskey Island mine, in light of the Morton Salt mine closure, were also not responded to. In 2020, two miners at a Cargill salt mine in Louisiana died while trying to prevent water from flooding the mine, according to lawsuits filed by family members.
Miners employed at the Fairport Harbor mine contacted by the Guardian declined to be interviewed, citing restrictions in a non-disclosure agreement.
For industry observers, the almost immediate decision to close Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine means that it might be time for monitoring authorities to step in.
“I would support a targeted, regulator-led review of water-intrusion risks at operating salt mines beneath the Great Lakes,” says Yu.

“[The Morton mine] incident is reason to check how each mine detects and responds to unusual seepage, and to review the condition of shafts and seals, the stability of roofs and pillars, and any known pathways from water-bearing rock.”

articles.title: Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather
articles.summary:
People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in…
articles.byline: Jonathan Watts; graphics by Sara Fiorillo

blocks.text: After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.
January Fourth-hottest January on record

blocks.caption: A fire in Longwood, a town in Victoria, Australia, in early January. Photograph: Michael Currie/AAP

blocks.text: Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.
February Fourth-hottest February on record

blocks.caption: People clear mud and debris outside homes in the aftermath of a storm, in Juiz de Fora, Brazil. Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPA

blocks.text: Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.
March Fourth-hottest March on record

blocks.caption: Motorists drive through heavy rains in the Kibera slums in Nairobi, Kenya.   Photograph: Donwilson Odhiambo/Getty Images

blocks.text: Devastating floods across much of the world In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.

World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.
April Second-hottest April on record

blocks.caption: A utility pole blocks a road in Saipan after a super typhoon with ferocious winds and relentless rains shredded tin roofs and forced people to take cover from flying tree limbs. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.
May Second-hottest May on record

blocks.caption: A man seeks relief from the heat as temperatures rise in New Delhi, India. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.
June Second-hottest June on record

blocks.caption: People assess the aftermath of landslides and flooding next to houses damaged in Attécoubé, a suburb of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. Photograph: Chris Boli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ocean heat enters uncharted territory Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.

Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.

West African deluge takes heavy toll Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.
after newsletter promotion
July Joint-hottest July on record

Fires choke Canada and Europe Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.

Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.
At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.
August Hottest August on record

Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.

Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.
September Second-hottest September on record

Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.
October Hottest October on record

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with police officers in Jakarta, Indonesia, during a demonstration against President Prabowo Subianto’s handling of forest fires. Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/Reuters

blocks.text: Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.

Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.

Roads turn to rivers in Chile After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.

Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.
November

blocks.caption: Global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives. Photograph: Jesús Vargas/Getty Images

blocks.text: 2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history

Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

articles.title: Why is Alberta ditching diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring practices?
articles.summary: Are hiring policies that strive for workplace diversity actually a problem that needs solving? Or is the UCP government engaging in political posturing? Panelists who spoke to CBC's West of Centre…

image.caption: Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery and Premier Danielle Smith talk to reporters about Bill 13, the Regulated Professions Neutrality Act, on Nov. 20, 2025. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Analysis

Are hiring policies that strive for workplace diversity actually a problem that needs solving? Or is the UCP government engaging in political posturing? Panelists who spoke to CBC's West of Centre are split on the answer.
CBC’s West of Centre podcast finds division on the issue
The Alberta government says eliminating diversity, equity and inclusion from public sector hiring will make sure employers are using a merit-based system.

But is it addressing a genuine problem that needs solving? Or is it, as the Opposition NDP argues, political posturing? CBC’s West of Centre spoke to experts and politics watchers who are split on the answer.

In a news conference last month, Premier Danielle Smith and Justice Minister Mickey Amery said the government's merit-based hiring bill is going to make the process more fair while ensuring the best-qualified candidates are selected.
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has called the move a doubling down on the “culture war” that doesn’t address the priorities of voters.
But the premier’s executive director, Bruce McAllister, posted on social media to describe scenarios where candidates are chosen for their race or sexuality rather than experience.
“It’s racist. It is discrimination against straight people, white people, Chinese people, Christians,” part of the post reads.
Diversity, equity and inclusion is a framework that aims to promote fair treatment and participation for people of all walks of life. It’s commonly referred to as DEI or EDI for short.

The Alberta bill would target hiring policies like one that was well-documented at the University of Alberta. It said if two candidates were equally qualified for a position, the hiring panels should favour the person from a historically underrepresented group.
The university changed the policy last spring after a provincial panel recommended post-secondary institutions adopt a culture of greater neutrality.

The bill is in addition to the “Peterson law,” also introduced by Smith and Amery last year, which eliminated mandatory DEI training from regulated professions. It was inspired by the 2022 sanctioning of author and academic Jordan Peterson by the psychology regulator in Ontario.
Is it American influence?

A large-scale walking back of DEI commitments made headlines in January 2025 when U.S. President Donald Trump signed sweeping executive orders against equity programs. A number of major private American companies followed suit with their own rollbacks.
Two years later, says Calgary-based DEI consultant Hagir Sail, there is a MAGA effect of quiet rollbacks happening — but plenty of resistance to DEI is homegrown.
“People, when they feel that life has become more difficult or don't have the same opportunities they used to have, they start pointing at the other,” Sail said.
Sail pushes back against the Albera government’s narrative that DEI means lower standards in hiring decisions.
“It's irresponsible to think that biases and systemic barriers don't play a role in keeping people at a lower place than they are.”
What do voters think?
But is scrapping DEI something that most Canadians support? It depends how you ask the question.

A Leger poll in 2024 suggested support has softened for DEI hiring in Canada. When asked if companies should take cultural background into account when hiring, 57 per cent of Canadian respondents said no, 28 per cent said yes.

But then when you ask Canadians more generally if they think the policies have a net positive impact on society or if DEI at work is a good thing, over 50 per cent say yes. That’s from 2025 polling from Abacus and the Environics Institute.
The Alberta Union of Provincial Employees has said that DEI hiring practices were never used in a way that would be unfair or encourage bias.

Leela Aheer, a former UCP deputy leader and cabinet minister, spoke to CBC West of Centre host Kathleen Petty. Aheer says DEI helps recruit the best people and this legislation is out of touch with voters who want unity. (Diane Yanko/CBC)
Leela Aheer, a former deputy leader and cabinet minister in Jason Kenney's UCP government, said rather than addressing a problem worth solving, the bill sends a worrisome message to some Albertans.

“Now you're campaigning on the backs of vulnerable people,” Aheer said. “And when it lands right after the referendum that told immigrants that their place here was up for a vote, what does that do to us as a province?”
Erika Barootes, a former principal secretary to Danielle Smith, said DEI policies were introduced to solve a problem but have ended up becoming one.
“We had good intentions, but that pendulum swung so damn far that now it's about correcting it.”
“And a lot of people are just like, ‘Thank goodness, someone's doing it.’”
Beyond Alberta
Smith isn’t alone in challenging the policy — freshly elected premiers coast to coast are showing a similar resistance to DEI.

Quebec’s Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has been critical of ‘wokeism,’ calling it anti-democratic. B.C. Conservative Lorne Doerkson’s platform promised to “restore merit-based hiring across the public sector.”

The debate has also been playing out quietly at the federal level. The standing committee on science and research recently released a report recommending that DEI not be used in awarding federal research funding and that demographic quotas or targets get banned.

One of the people called as a witness to the committee is Dave Snow, an associate professor of political science at the University of Guelph. Snow said DEI in university research has gone too far, taking on what he describes as an activist tone that comes at the expense of research excellence.
But Snow said he doesn’t anticipate sweeping changes in the federal public service or academia.
“I think the commitment to EDI is really strong and I think if anything...the Trump administration's really strong attacks on EDI has hardened the resolve of Canadian universities.”

As for the Alberta bill, once it receives royal assent and comes into force it will change the way provincial public agencies are able to hire: including Crown corporations, post-secondary institutions, school boards and municipalities.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emily is a reporter and producer with CBC's West of Centre podcast. Previously, she covered Edmonton city hall. She can be reached at emily.williams@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Philippines to host ASEAN Maritime Center - DFA
articles.summary: The ASEAN Maritime Center is set to be established in the Philippines, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) announced on Saturday.

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 8:49pm
The ASEAN Maritime Center is set to be established in the Philippines, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) announced on Saturday.
DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro made the announcement during a press briefing at the International Media Center in Pasay City.
"During the foreign ministers' meeting, we adopted the concept note. The terms of reference of the ASEAN Maritime Center will be based in the Philippines," Lazaro said.
"We haven't really decided all the other issues concerning this, but this is a very important result of our chairship," she added.
Lazaro said the center will serve as a knowledge hub and support platform for maritime-related initiatives and issues, in line with the priorities identified by ASEAN member states.
"It involves issues on port authorities. It involves the whole gamut of the blue economy," she said.
In a previous statement, Lazaro underscored the need to strengthen maritime security and cooperation among ASEAN member states. —VBL, GMA News

"This is one of the fundamental issues in our trade negotiation, and we are making progress toward that," he said of the auto sector, adding it was also "one of the most challenging issues" in the talks.

Carney revealed he had "quite a long, substantive conversation" this week with U.S. President Donald Trump, in which both U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Trump's chief of staff Stephen Miller were on the line.
Carney said the American automotive market relies in part on Canadian manufacturing, and the continental industry is challenged by speed of production and by electrification.

"The sooner that we can get to a stable trading relationship under the new trade policy of the United States for the auto sector, it's absolutely in the interest of course of Canadian workers, Canadian auto sector, but very much the U.S. as well," he said.

items: Feds, Ontario offering Stellantis 'aggressive package' to keep Brampton auto plant open

blocks.text: Carney also said that Chinese investment in Canada's auto sector is restricted to a set timeline and amount of vehicles, and will be reassessed based on multiple factors including the state of Canada's integration into the U.S. automotive sector.

The prime minister also reiterated that Ottawa feels automaker Stellantis has not met obligations it took when accepting federal funds, following this week's announcement of a deal to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.
"We're not satisfied in any way with the current situation and the partial approach that Stellantis has taken here," Carney said.
"The expectation is that Stellantis fully respects its engagements to the workers and to Canada."

articles.title: From micro to massive, ASEAN’s entrepreneurs face regulatory hurdles
articles.summary: ‘It's incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,’ former CIMB chairman Nazir Razak says, criticizing ASEAN’s slow progress toward…

blocks.text: BIG BUSINESS. Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala speaks during a panel at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on November 14, 2026.
Rappler

‘It's incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,’ former CIMB chairman Nazir Razak says, criticizing ASEAN’s slow progress toward economic integration

items: Joey Concepcion, founder of Go Negosyo, advocates for more lenient regulations for microentrepreneurs, emphasizing the importance of support for small businesses.
Larger businesses also face regulatory challenges as they expand across Southeast Asia, with differing national standards complicating investment and operational processes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A food vendor at a weekend bazaar might have little in common with a conglomerate investing across Southeast Asia, yet both can find themselves grappling with regulations that make growing their business harder than it should be.
For Go Negosyo founder Joey Concepcion, governments should give microentrepreneurs some wiggle room, particularly when they are just starting out.
Speaking on the sidelines of the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on Saturday, November 14, Concepcion recalled how he began his own entrepreneurial journey.

“When I started as an entrepreneur, I didn’t apply for any permit,” he said, also pointing out that many successful food vendors at bazaars sometimes sell products without certificates of product registration.

blocks.caption: From micro to massive, ASEAN’s entrepreneurs face regulatory hurdles

blocks.text: Concepcion knows a thing or two about building a business. He heads RFM Corporation, which is behind the Selecta ice cream Filipinos love, while his family’s other business, Concepcion Industrial, makes the Condura refrigerators that keep it cold. Through Go Negosyo, he has also spent years helping fledgling entrepreneurs get their businesses off the ground.
“If I were the government, I’d just let it go for now and allow them to continue. And eventually, they will gradually follow the rules,” he said. “It cannot be too strict in the process though.”

Beyond permits, Concepcion said small entrepreneurs also struggle with financing and developing better products. This is where mentorship becomes important, particularly in helping businesses become viable enough to qualify for bank loans.
Larger businesses also have a stake in their success. After all, Concepcion noted, sari-sari stores are important outlets for products sold by major manufacturers.
“Because if they close shop, then our sales obviously will also go down,” he said.

blocks.caption: [Good Business] Sari-sari stores: Kapwa at play amid economic crises

blocks.text: The difficulty of navigating regulations does not disappear as businesses grow; it only changes. Across ASEAN, even its most successful businessmen still grapple with differing national standards, investment approvals, and employment requirements.
Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala said these differences complicate efforts to expand across the region, despite the complementary strengths of Southeast Asian economies.

“There’s still a lot that needs to be done,” he said during a separate panel. “How we would like as a company to be able to move within these different countries in a much easier way, but the standards that we have, the approval standards, the way to get your investment filed, it’s different in each of these countries.”

blocks.caption: From micro to massive, ASEAN’s entrepreneurs face regulatory hurdles

blocks.text: Malaysian banker Nazir Razak, former CIMB Group chairman, had stronger words for ASEAN’s slow progress toward economic integration.
“It’s incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,” he said.

Nazir recalled how CIMB expanded across Southeast Asia in anticipation of the ASEAN Economic Community, launched in 2015 to great fanfare and with the ambition of establishing a single market and production base.
“I felt we were all dressed up with nowhere to go,” he said.

ASEAN has nevertheless continued attracting investment. Foreign direct investment rose 10% to a record $246 billion in 2025, according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2026. Investment originating within the regional bloc also grew 34% to $40 billion, accounting for 16% of total inflows.

Still, Nazir feels that ASEAN has plenty more unlocked economic potential, but its leadership structure could be holding it back. He criticized how much of the authority rests with the chair, which changes every year, rather than the secretary-general, who serves a five-year term. He argued that the arrangement needed reform to help the bloc move faster.
“So you imagine a company where all power is with the chairman, but the chairman changes every year. That would be completely dysfunctional,” he said.
The Philippines is set to hand over ASEAN’s rotating chairmanship to Singapore for 2027. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Microsoft services fully restored after global outage
articles.summary: Microsoft said on Saturday that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications ‌for businesses and governments…

image.caption: Microsoft says it has fully resolved a global outage that affected millions of its users worldwide. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·New

Microsoft said on Saturday that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications ‌for businesses and governments for over 24 hours.
Microsoft had said server issues were behind the problem and that it was not aware of any malicious activity
"We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company posted on X.
Microsoft had said server issues were behind the problem that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause.

Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications, with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending ​emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.
Microsoft apologizes for global outage as services come back online

It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, ​caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.
Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.
Another outage for Microsoft
The outage, reports of which started climbing Thursday, ​is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year.
Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based ⁠email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational.
The incident ⁠deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software ‌and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.

items: Microsoft gives voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees

blocks.text: It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft's workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector's parent company, Ookla.
Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.
"It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider's email and collaboration tools," said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla.
Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 on Friday. The stock has gained roughly eight per cent so far this year.

Disruptions and ⁠financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice-president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the outage at between $300 million and $500 million, well below the $400 million to $1.5 billion financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than eight million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.

Microsoft also faced an outage with ‌its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.
"The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year," said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro.
"If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider's hands."
Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push ​customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations.

articles.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England economist says
articles.summary:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% last month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and…

blocks.text: The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

Pill told the Financial Times: “My view would be, we will see evidence that motivates further rises,” adding that the central bank would “do ‌what is necessary to get inflation back to 2% through time”.
The chief economist is one of a number of the Bank’s policymakers who believe the UK economy has gained in strength over the last year, handing workers the power to bid up wages.
Recent figures showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, to give an annual rate of growth that was only surpassed by the US among the G7 group of wealthy countries.

With inflation expected to rise to 5% in spring next year, driven by high oil and gas prices as a result of the Iran war, Pill expects public and private sector workers to demand substantial pay rises, which would keep inflation high for a longer period.

Pill said he considered an end to the US-Israeli ‌conflict with Iran and a fall in energy prices to be a “very low probability”, signalling to the newspaper that he was poised to vote for another ​quarter-point increase next month.

“My bias, for what it’s worth, is that I worry about the inflationary impact being magnified by second-round effects,” he said, adding that he believed the central bank should have acted sooner to combat inflation. “In my ⁠view, we waited too long.”
While the Bank has not seen evidence of wage increases or companies being able to pass on higher costs to consumers, Pill said the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence.
“As we go into next year, we will begin to see some evidence, and it could play out in one direction or another — we’ll see.”
after newsletter promotion

Financial markets expect UK interest rates to rise to almost 5% in 2027. Pill said these expectations were “not outrageous”, hinting that he could vote for more substantial increases in the cost of borrowing at the next meetings of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) because the “ability to be ​modest [in the scale ​of rate rises] has diminished”.

City analysts have interpreted the increasingly hawkish comments of Pill and other MPC members as making an interest rate rise in December almost inevitable. But there is disagreement about the strength of the economy, with many concerned that further increases in the cost of borrowing will hit the manufacturing sector and the construction industry, which has contracted for much of the year.

Households are also likely to cut back on spending in the new year, when the energy price cap is expected to rise to almost £2,000 for a typical home and council tax bills increase by an average of almost 5%.
