articles.title: Not good enough for the 27 Club
articles.summary: 'Greatness wasn’t my gift, but the potential for it. Now, I think that is somehow worse.'

blocks.text: I was never a Promil Kid. I was never on the cover of a newspaper or a magazine. All I knew was that my parents believed in me.

Growing up, I always felt like I was on the verge of greatness. I was not exactly the most outstanding student. I was never No. 1 (and to be honest, often not even No. 2), but I was usually somewhere up there.
So you could say greatness wasn’t my gift, but the potential for it. But now I think that is somehow worse.

In preschool, I think what made me stand out was my unusual worldliness for someone who was not even five. If iPad kids surprise you nowadays with their ability to name country capitals and their uncanny accents that sound too close to Peppa Pig, that was me before it was “trendy.”

I would talk to my parents’ peers about Fisherman’s Wharf in San Francisco thanks to 5 am reruns of Scooby-Doo — which I was already up for, since I had to travel from Cavite to Las Piñas to school daily.

In elementary school, they would ask me to recite Greek Gods, their Roman counterparts, and the words born from their names. When they asked me what I wanted to be when I grew up, I would say “Paleontologist,” and they would react: PaLEONtoLogist? (Yes, it also elicited those reactions before it even became a thing). All things considered, from preschool onwards, people already called me a “human encyclopedia.”

My “first-born” energy showed in how I never shied away from the spotlight. Quiz bees and declamation contests, the odd VTR here and there, being a literal poster child, guest appearances on a chocolate drink-sponsored children’s show on national TV (I would tell you the name of the show if only ’90s Philippine TV archives weren’t a lost-media wasteland). Basically, I was unafraid of being “out there,” if one of those white vans from urban legend needed a child volunteer, I might’ve raised my hand.

I began to think that being impressive for my age meant being destined to impress everyone, and this continued until my pre-adolescence. As my school uniform switched from slack shorts to actual slacks, my pop culture consumption also changed. It went beyond cartoons and the spreadsheets about them (such a nerd), and moved into music, history, and the arts. This is when I first encountered “The 27 Club.”
Again, I wasn’t the smartest kid growing up, but smart doesn’t always mean gifted, and gifted doesn’t always mean great.

I never set my sights then on being a doctor, lawyer, or artist of those “de-kahon” dreams. No, what I wanted was to be “great.” I didn’t care what word succeeded it — “great (blank)” — I just knew I wanted to be it.

I was a creative, but not in any particular field. I drew well, sang okay, and wrote with words that weren’t exactly hifalutin, but were at a reading level higher than my age. I thought I had the potential for greatness, not because of my innate skills but because of what people told me. You grow up with enough people saying, “you could” and not “you are,” and you really end up believing it.

When I learned about the “27 Club,” or the selected few supposedly in the upper echelons of greatness whose stories always ended with “gone too soon,” what resonated most with me was that lost potential. People already cared about what they’d made, yet they always fixated on what they could still have done. Potential survived beyond 27.

To be honest, my immature appreciation in art even deluded me into thinking I had comparable talent to these greats, because I thought they weren’t exactly the most traditionally talented. Janis Joplin didn’t exactly have a voice that would turn chairs in The Voice; Basquiat’s painting didn’t look much better than my editorial cartoons for the school paper.

Reaching 27 then became a tangible threat. I had 11-14 years to discover what I was really meant to do and become super good at it; that meant I would die at age 27. As problematic as it may sound, it felt like: “If I die at 27. After that, then I’ll know that I’ve made it.” I had confused dying young with having done enough to be mourned.
Fast forward to my first real heartbreak.

During my fourth year of high school, when I was applying to universities, I thought, “Yeah, I might not be graduating with the highest honors, but accolades in high school — especially one in a province like Cavite — it’s child’s play; nobody really cares about dat shit.” And I already knew what “peaked in high school” meant all those years ago. College, that’s the true battleground. So, beam me up, Scotty. I’m ready.

But then the beam never came. I didn’t pass my first-choice course: Film in UP Diliman. Though, to be honest, I just selected that course because my mom said, “You like watching movies, right? Naturally, you’ll be a good director.”
Anyway, that was the first rejection that actually hurt. I passed all the other universities: Ateneo, La Salle, UST. But not UP Diliman. I got into UP Los Baños, not Diliman.
I never regretted going to UPLB, and ultimately didn’t choose to move to Diliman when I had the option; I think this was the first time that I actually questioned my potential.
I became quite popular in college. But that first pain of rejection led me down a path where, if I didn’t think I’d be a star at it, I chose not to do it at all. (Even unconsciously.)

Being a good writer meant submitting a piece for the Palancas. But you know, “I’m too busy with actual journalism to write essays and fiction.” My teachers would say, ” Apply for highly selective international exchange programs.” But “I’m too busy being the student council president of our college,” I would tell them.
As long as I didn’t submit, I could still imagine winning.

Potential goes both ways. And it’s better not to know than to actually know. Better to let them think, “sayang, pasok ka dun sana (What a waste, you would have surely gotten in),” than to be actually certain that I didn’t make the cut.

Still, I graduated college with honors, leadership distinctions, and some other extracurricular stuff. At UP, this was just okay, not the best, not enough to get your face on a social media card. But it felt like a step in the right direction. The rush of those four years in college was just enough to fill that “Early Life” tab on the Wikipedia page that was surely destined for my name.

If college was my first heartbreak, then after college was the real battleground — where it opened the floodgates to doubt, existentialism, and ego death. I felt good when there was some sort of road map, but when I was left to fend for myself out in the field, I wriggled like a worm after the rain.

I was lucky enough then to get into Leo Burnett’s management trainee program. Inside it, I thought, “Oh, my goal now, my path to greatness, was to be one of the youngest at the Cannes Lions.” “For sure, I would be in France the next year.” “No gold yet for the Philippines? For sure, I’d not only bring it home, but be the youngest ever to do so.”
But come the End of the Year Party, when awards were being given out, not even “Face of the Night” was reserved for me. (I hope that award keeps you warm at night, Toby Amigo).
Soon, I left advertising for journalism. I started doing film criticism. I was already 24 then. “3 years left, kaya pa yan! (I’ve still got this!).”

My entry into Rappler was already one for the history books. I joined Rappler on January 15, 2018. On January 15, 2018, the Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) published its decision to revoke Rappler’s operating license.

Of course, this didn’t mean a new level of impunity for the Duterte government, as journalists were now a target. No, this was merely meant to be the cold open of a hero coming to save the little newsroom that could. “Step aside, Maria Ressa, narito na ang Lisan Al-Ghaib. (The Lisan Al-Ghaib is here.)”

Truthfully though, I was already antsy. Two years of creative toil didn’t land me any mention on Young Star. I tried and failed to get into Berlinale as a film critic. When they shot the documentary A Thousand Cuts, I didn’t even get any speaking roles. (I’m the guy doing a toast during the last frames of the film, though. *Self-high-five*).

Time flew, and I was now 27. But just as I was feeling the rush of time, everything ground to a halt in 2020. Maybe the universe took my request to slow things down a little too literally. Between 27 and 30, amid the global pandemic, my parents became senior citizens, and on the cusp of my 30th, I chose to adult and put on my big-boy pants.
A lot has changed since then. I know there’s something in those intervening worth writing about, but, as I tell my writing teachers, it’s “not that deep.”

On paper, those years look pretty good. I’ve worked in regional corporate roles. I’ve traveled around while reporting to headquarters in Singapore. I’ve lived in India for a little over a year. And now, I’m based in the UAE.

I know they say that the grass is always greener. And, there truly is much to be thankful for; many would happily wear my “success” as a badge of honor. But to me, it feels like packing up my crayons, erasing the colors I drew beyond the edges, and being the “de-kahon” that I never imagined myself for myseLf.
At 33, I write this at a workshop, reading to my classmates my history of delusions, and how much I ponder upon unrealized potential and the possible alternate permutations of my decisions.

It’s not all lost, though. Truly, I’m not sad, just sober. And when I think of how unfit today I would be for the club of 27, I just remember what my workshop seatmate last week, Tita Beng, said to me: “Don’t worry. Jesus and Jose Rizal* died when they were 33.” – Rappler.com
*Turns out Jose Rizal died at 35. Sorry, Tita Beng, two years to go.
Note: This essay was originally the output for Jessica Zafra’s “Writing Boot Camp: Memoirs.”

articles.title: Canadian judge decries U.S. sanctions of International Criminal Court as 'attack in favour of impunity'
articles.summary: Kimberly Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court, was sanctioned by the Trump administration last August. Despite impacts including cancelled credit cards and frozen bank…
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Terence McKenna, Alex Shprintsen

blocks.text: World·New

Kimberly Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court, was sanctioned by the Trump administration last August. Despite impacts including cancelled credit cards and frozen bank accounts, she says attempts to intimidate her and other court officials are 'futile.'
Winnipeg-born Kimberly Prost and other ICC officials sanctioned last August
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 14, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago
The ICC will survive Trump's attacks, Canadian judge says
Kimberly Prost began to feel the effects of the U.S. sanctions immediately.
"These economic sanctions are not symbolic in any way," said Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), who was sanctioned by the Trump administration last year.
Prost's credit cards were cancelled and her access to banking services hindered, she said, because of the U.S.'s wide-reaching impact on the global banking system.
"Every time literally I go to make a bank transfer, I hold my breath because I don't know if it's going to work," Prost said in an interview with CBC News.
"To order an Uber, book a hotel, buy a theatre ticket — everything requires some form of credit card, and so you're sort of struggling to adjust."
Google, iCloud, Amazon accounts cut off for ICC judges amid U.S. sanctions

Based in The Hague, Netherlands, the ICC investigates and tries individuals charged with genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when courts in its 125 member states, including Canada, are unwilling or unable to do so.

The sanctions on Prost are part of a larger U.S. campaign to discredit and dismantle the ICC, which began in earnest after a February 2025 executive order imposed sanctions for investigating American personnel and issuing arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

U.S. President Donald Trump has since sustained his attack on the international court, calling on member states to immediately "resign from this rogue institution" in a September UN General Assembly speech. Just last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio threatened to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" if allies do not "rein in" the court.

In a Sept. 22, 2026, speech at the United Nations General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump urged member nations of the International Criminal Court to 'officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.' (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)
Prost says these actions are an attack against the international system of criminal justice and rule of law that has been built since the Second World War.

"It is an attack that foresees a world where victims of atrocity crimes are forgotten. And it is an attack in favour of impunity and ending accountability for these crimes. That's the only way it can be framed."
Rubio warns ICC endangers Americans
Prost was singled out for her role in judicially authorizing a March 2020 preliminary investigation into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan since 2003, including by U.S. service members.
Since 2021, however, the investigation has deprioritized the role of the U.S., focusing instead on the Afghan government and Taliban forces.
"To my knowledge, there's no active investigation of the Americans in that case, but I'm sanctioned."

items: Trump administration sanctions Canadian judge who sits on International Criminal Court

blocks.text: The United States has never been a member of the ICC, and has long expressed concerns that its citizens could be prosecuted.

"As the United States works to bring peace around the world, our diplomats or our soldiers could be drawn into this court," President George W. Bush said the day after the court was inaugurated in 2002. "It's very troubling to me."

Twenty-four years later, Rubio echoed the same rhetoric about the "dangers" of the global court, warning that American border patrol agents, marines and prosecutors would "be at the mercy of foreign judges," risking imprisonment for defending their own country.

However, Prost says Rubio's arguments are misleading, as the ICC would have "no jurisdiction" if the U.S. asserted its sovereignty and conducted its own genuine investigations or prosecutions when allegations arise.
Member states 'have to protect' ICC

Prost and two other ICC judges sued the Trump administration in June, opposing the sanctions that they say are "designed to exert extra-judicial pressure" and coerce them into "prioritizing their private interests over deciding cases on the basis of the law and facts."
"We decided that it was so significant and such an impediment to our work — and to the work of the court — to challenge it before the courts of the United States," said Prost.

In July, four former U.S. ambassadors and prosecutors of international criminal tribunals submitted a brief in support of the ICC judges, arguing that the sanctions "penalize independent judicial decision-making."

items: Ottawa tight-lipped on joining legal case against Trump sanction of Canadian ICC judge

blocks.text: Canadian officials have not intervened in Prost's lawsuit. But in a September interview with CBC News, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said Canada "remains committed to the ICC process."

"As a sovereign country, we determine our foreign policy, and that includes the principles on which our foreign policy is based," Anand said. "One of those fundamental principles is respect for international law."
Mission of ICC 'too important' to abandon, says Canadian judge
Prost said the efforts to intimidate her and other judges are ultimately "futile."
"We continue to judge our cases on the facts and the law and the evidence before us objectively and independently, and that will never change," she said.

In October, the U.S. allowed the ICC to access certain information technology and banking services for six months. The State Department said that time would allow member states to demonstrate "meaningful progress" on U.S. concerns.

items: EU awards human rights prize to International Criminal Court amid Trump attacks
Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions

blocks.text: Prost says losing access to those systems could have a "very crippling effect" on the court's operations.
Though some member states have signaled support, she says the moment remains "critically important" to safeguard the ICC, which has taken steps to prepare in case sanctions come into full force.
"It's their court. It's not the prosecutors' court, not the judges' court. It's the states' court, and they have to protect it."
With files from Reuters and The Canadian Press

articles.title: 4 decades ago, Robert Munsch attended Moira Green's birthday. Her story became a children's classic
articles.summary: Four decades ago, Robert Munsch flew to the Northwest Territories in search of inspiration. The beloved author found it at Moira Green's sixth birthday party.

image.caption: Moira Green, right, is seen here at her sixth party in Hay River, N.W.T. Author Robert Munsch was staying with the Green family and told a story that would become the book Moira's Birthday, left. (Annick Press/Submitted by Moira Green)

blocks.text: On Moira Green’s 10th birthday, she put on a giant paper bag and a homemade crown and headed down to Hay River’s public library, where a surprising number of residents from the remote Northwest Territories town were waiting.

There were 200 pizzas and 200 little cakes. She ran into a dragon, Prince Ronald and other valiant attempts by her Grade 5 classmates to bring the beloved characters from Robert Munsch’s earliest works to life.
Technically, Green could have come dressed as herself: the inspiration behind Moira’s Birthday.

“After we did our little performances and stuff, they got Robert Munsch on the line,” Green said in a recent interview. “I don't know how they did it back in the day, but everyone in the library could hear him. And then, he read the story [to] all of us."
It was November 1987.

Six months earlier, Toronto-based Annick Press had published Moira’s Birthday. And exactly four years previous, the Guelph, Ont., children’s author had visited the Northwest Territories for the first time, leaving behind a trail of memories for many in the community of roughly 3,500 people living there at the time, and, as Green recalls, whenever anyone new turned up, her parents insisted they come for supper.

That small-town friendliness was how Munsch, known for billeting with families during his tours, came to stay with Bruce and Marilyn Green and their five children, all of whom would make an appearance in the first of three books he would dream up during the trip.

Green, shown wearing the Paper Bag Princess costume, is seen here at her 10th birthday party in Hay River, N.W.T., in November 1987. She and other kids performed skits based on Munsch's books. (Submitted by Moira Green)

Those connections Munsch forged with kids, living in big cities and tiny hamlets, became the fabric of the nearly 100 books he has written in his career. In an interview with CBC News last year, his “last hurrah,” the author revealed that another 50 books will likely be published after his death.
As first reported in the New York Times in September 2025, Munsch has been approved for medical assistance in dying (MAID), when he chooses. He has been living with Parkinson’s disease and dementia.

“Nobody lives forever," he told CBC in December. “But I will at least have a couple of years, as many years as I’ve already had [after I’m gone], and that will be nice," he said, of his hope to publish a book per year after his death.
Munsch and his wife, Ann, who have been married for more than five decades, are shown here at their home in November 2025. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)
The breadth of his travels helped him capture what it was like to be a kid in a country as vast as Canada.
Even in a place as remote as Hay River.
Moira’s 6th birthday

On the morning of her sixth birthday party in November 1983, Green and her siblings went to see Munsch perform at the library. He captivated his audience, she said, despite having just flown in hours before from Yellowknife.
Her party had already been planned for that afternoon before news of Munsch’s visit came out.
It was not quite as raucous as the story suggests — a handful of friends, not the whole school, showed up. And during a quiet moment, her dad walked over.
“He said ‘You should ask Mr. Munsch if he could tell you a story.’ And I was like, ‘Mmmm, I'm not going to do that. I'm way too shy.’”
Green, left, shown in her Grade 1 photo, which helped artist Michael Martchenko illustrate the book, shown right. (Submitted by Moira Green/Annick Press)
But a friend did it for her, she said. The author recalls that he couldn’t refuse.

“Sometimes when a kid asks me to make up a story, I get this strange feeling that something is going to happen,” Munsch wrote of the experience. “I look out at a group of kids and get this firm conviction that I can tell a new story about a particular kid.
“Usually, it’s not true, but I do always try a new story when I get the feeling.”

items: 'The stories will be the last thing to go': Robert Munsch on his legacy as one of Canada's great storytellers
Beloved children's author Robert Munsch promising dozens of books to come after his death

blocks.text: Green was just as surprised, as she had assumed he would retell a previous story.
“But he came over … sat down and then he just sort of started telling — making up — the story on the spot: Moira’s Birthday.
Anyone who has heard Munsch perform knows how he revs up a crowd, along with his own volume, asking questions and weaving the answers into his words.
“Lots of interactions, stopping to talk about the local bakery and, you know, other things from around town and kind of integrate that into the story."
Even before he finished, Munsch said, he knew he had a winner.

He added Green to his “Story Kids file" and asked if he could stay in touch, both recalled. Illustrator Michael Martchenko followed up, looking for pictures of the family, their green house and even the dog.
The Green family's home, shown here in the 1980s, in Hay River, N.W.T. It became part of the iconic story. (Submitted by Moira Green)
“We heard later that he had continued to tell that story,” Green said, “kind of fine-tuning it and shaping it as he does by telling it to the kids and gauging their reaction."
When Munsch sent her an early draft, Green saw the story had evolved.
In the first rendition, she had received money in all of her presents. And she said she used the money to either pay for the massive order of pizza and cake — or paid her guests to help clean up.
"There was a little bit of a difference in how the story kind of tied up.”

In the published version, Moira’s beleaguered parents look at the destruction of their home. Then, the birthday girl announces that anyone who helps clean up will get one of her (many, many) presents. Within minutes, the house is spotless.
Robert Munsch has a lot more stories to tell
Reconnecting as an adult
Green and the author stayed in touch, exchanging Christmas cards, letters and signed copies of new books.

“Sometimes, he would even send manuscripts of a potential story, asking for feedback,” she said. “It was kind of a neat world to be a part of at that point — you sort of joined the Robert Munsch family."

Each of Munsch’s books — which have sold more than 90 million copies in North America alone — is dedicated to the child who inspired it. Several feature his own children: Tyya, Andrew and Julie. In fact, Julie’s decision to invite far more kids than she was allowed to contributed to the narrative behind Moira’s Birthday, the author writes.

Others, like Green, continued corresponding with Munsch — like Gah-Ning Tang, the protagonist in Where is Gah-Ning, whose letters spanned more than 30 years, leading her to eventually refer to the author and his wife as uncle and aunt, she told CBC’s Day 6 in a 2025 interview.
LISTEN | How a Hearst, Ont., girl came to call Munsch her uncle:
Day 614:06Gah-Ning Tang reflects on a lifetime of correspondence with Robert Munsch and his book that bears her name
Green lost touch shortly after university, she said.
Then, as a young mother in Saskatoon, she saw that Munsch was coming into town for a performance. She brought her daughter and reconnected with him afterward.
“He spent some time with us and was thrilled,” Green said. They exchanged contact information and he got in touch before his next trip to the city.
Green loved reading her copies of Munsch’s books to her four children, though “mine wasn’t necessarily their favourite,” she said, laughing.
Watch world-renowned storyteller Robert Munsch perform The Paper Bag Princess
As she celebrates her 49th birthday this month, she recalls being a shy kid who didn’t always appreciate the attention.
Now, though, she said she “can recognize the cool factor” in all of it.
“It’s my go-to icebreaker.”

articles.title: Minimum wage hasn't kept pace with the cost of living across Canada, new reports show
articles.summary: Of the 59 cities and regions in reports for every province reviewed by CBC News, none had a provincial minimum wage equal to the calculated living wage — the amount a full-time worker needs to meet…

image.caption: Volunteers at the Daily Bread Food Bank, in Toronto on Nov. 3. Canadian food bank usage hit record highs this year as new reports show that provincial minimum wages fall below the living wages coast to coast. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

blocks.text: Minimum wage hasn't kept pace with the cost of living across Canada amid high food prices, rents and other everyday necessities, according to a series of new reports.

Of the 59 cities and regions in the reports for every province reviewed by CBC News, none had a provincial minimum wage equal to the calculated living wage — the amount a full-time worker needs to meet their basic needs.

A gap between the two wages means a person working full-time at minimum wage would not be able to cover their basic expenses. Some of the widest gaps were found in Alberta, which has the lowest minimum wage in the country, and in parts of Nova Scotia, where living wages were driven up in some areas by significant rises in rental costs.

Brandon, Man., had just a $1 gap between its estimated $17.40 living wage and $16.40 provincial minimum wage, according to data published by the Manitoba Federation of Labour on Sept. 28. But on the other end of the spectrum, Montreal; Halifax; the northern peninsula of Labrador; Banff, Alta.; and Whitehorse had some of the widest gaps, each between $12 and $14.

Taken as a whole, the data suggests the wage floor has been permitted to "lag considerably" behind the cost of providing for the basic necessities of life, says Tom McDowell, a lecturer in politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University.
"The minimum wage is a political measure that is largely disconnected from the actual costs of living," McDowell, who researchers living wage and basic income, told CBC News.
"The failure of the minimum wage to keep up with the rising costs of essentials can help to explain why so many households today are falling short on basic needs."
Halifax living wage $30 an hour: report
What's a living wage?

A living wage represents the hourly income required to cover basic expenses like shelter, food, transportation and child care, with enough buffer to avoid chronic financial stress and manage unexpected expenses, and to participate meaningfully in society — all based on the actual costs in that person's community.
It assumes each adult is working 35 hours per week, and considers government transfers and tax deductions, according to the Alberta Living Wage Report, released last week.

"It is also a conservative, bare-bones budget without the extras many of us take for granted," said the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives in its recent living wage update for Regina and Saskatoon.

CBC News reviewed data from nine separate provincial and regional reports compiled by different organizations, though they didn't all use the exact same methodologies to calculate living wage. Montreal's, for instance, is based on a single-person household, while the reports for Ontario, Alberta and B.C. use a weighted average of different household types.

items: Maple Leaf Foods to raise prices again early next year, CEO says
About half of workers in N.S. and N.L. earning less than the living wage: report
Minimum wage rate 'not cutting it,' says Ontario Living Wage Network

blocks.text: In addition, some reports looked at specific cities, while others looked more broadly at regions. There was also no current data available for Nunavut or the Northwest Territories. So the city comparisons shouldn't be interpreted as a definitive ranking between provinces or territories.
Still, the fact remains that in all the data that's available from coast to coast, the living wage surpasses the minimum wage — and the living wage is climbing in most areas.
Struggling to get by? Here’s why minimum wage doesn’t cover the cost of living

For instance, in Whitehorse, the living wage jumped 13.3 per cent from 2025, according to the Yukon Anti-Poverty Coalition. And provincial average living wages increased just under four per cent in Nova Scotia, 5.75 per cent in P.E.I., and and 7.39 per cent in Newfoundland and Labrador compared to 2025, according to a new report from the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.
Who isn't earning a living wage in Canada?

All told, it means there's a significant proportion of Canadians unable to raise themselves out of poverty even if they're working full time, says Molly McCracken, the Manitoba director at the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.
"These are more likely to be women, immigrants and racialized people because that's just how the labour force is stratified," McCracken said.

In Metro Vancouver, for instance, 35 per cent of all employees earn less than the region’s living wage of $27.85 per hour, according to Living Wage B.C. The majority of them are women, and three-quarters are racialized. Nearly half of all racialized women working in Metro Vancouver earn less than the living wage, notes Living Wage B.C.'s May report.

On the other side of Canada, half of women workers in Newfoundland and Labrador do not receive a living wage, according to the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives. This includes many home-care workers and early childhood educators, the centre says.

Shelves at the North York Harvest Food Bank in Toronto on Oct. 20. A new report from the Salvation Army says nearly one in three Canadians is skipping or reducing meals because they can't afford groceries. (Frank Gunn/The Canadian Press)

In downtown St. John's, demand at the Bridges to Hope food bank is up this year by 20 per cent over last year, executive director Lesley Burgess said earlier this week, and she says inadequate incomes and high costs are driving the need.
"Food banks are designed to [provide] a few days of food to get you through an emergency until your next cheque comes," she said.
"The problem that we're seeing now is that the cheque coming is not enough to cover even the basics."
Canadian food bank usage hit record highs this year, and a new report from the Salvation Army says nearly one in three Canadians is skipping or reducing meals because they can't afford groceries.
So what needs to change?

The failure to provide an adequate living wage leaves workers chronically stretched to afford the basics of life, says McDowell, the lecturer at Toronto Metropolitan University. Some have to work additional hours or take on extra jobs to make ends meet.

The reality for those making about minimum wage may be even more dire than the data suggests, adds McCracken, because a living wage assumes someone is working full time. When more often, someone making a lower wage might be working part time or have precarious work with shifting schedules and no sick days.

So, what's the answer? The Canadian Federation of Independent Business told CBC News earlier this week that it isn't very realistic for many small- and medium-sized businesses to offer a living wage while lower profits and trade and tariff pressures are dampening bottom lines.

items: Toronto-area workers need at least $27.60/hour, group says
Canadian economy lost 4,700 jobs in October as unemployment rate hit 6.7%

blocks.text: McDowell says the minimum wage should be formally indexed to the local living-wage benchmark and to the actual costs of living, "rather than being left to the discretion of politicians and policymakers."
"The underlying principle, however, is that full-time work should be sufficient to cover the essentials of life," he said.

There are a lot of potential benefits to increasing provincial minimum wages, McCracken added, like less employee turnover and fewer costs to the public sector for resources like employment insurance. But there also needs to be better low-income supports, like tax breaks, rent control and stronger employment standards, she says.

Manitoba's minimum wage increased to $16.40 on Oct. 1. But even then, it falls about $4 short of the living wage in Winnipeg, which, as McCracken points out, was the site of the famous 1919 general strike.
"The fight for a living wage was one of the main asks of that movement and still to this day we're fighting for it," she said.
Alberta's living wage all over the map in 2026

articles.title: Is a cure on the horizon for hepatitis B? New drug offers hope, but there's a 'long way to go'
articles.summary: Is a cure on the horizon for hepatitis B? A newly-approved drug offers hope, but wiping out this viral liver infection remains a challenge.

image.caption: Hepatitis B virus, shown here, can lead to chronic liver disease. In early November, Health Canada approved a breakthrough drug offering the first 'functional cure' for some patients, though major questions remain about access, cost and how long its impacts last. (U.S. Centers for Disease Control an

blocks.text: This is an excerpt from Second Opinion, a weekly analysis of health and medical science news emailed to subscribers Saturday mornings. If you haven't subscribed yet, you can do that by clicking here.
Despite decades of efforts to wipe out hepatitis B, the viral liver infection remains a quiet threat — and one that's long lacked a cure.

While rates have dropped dramatically since the rise of childhood vaccination programs, an estimated 260,000 Canadians are still living with the virus, including roughly half who don't know they're infected. Over time, many of those silently carrying the virus go on to develop a range of life-threatening issues, including cancer or sudden liver failure.
Could a long-awaited cure finally be in sight?
In early November, Health Canada approved a breakthrough drug offering the first "functional cure" for a portion of chronic hepatitis B patients, which drugmaker GSK expect to roll out in early 2027.
Dr. Carla Coffin, a hepatologist and professor at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, calls it a "major step forward."

At the same time, she warned it's only effective in a relatively small proportion of people with hepatitis B — and questions remain around cost, access and just how long the impacts of the powerful new treatment last.
Virus can lead to chronic liver infection

The hepatitis B virus spreads through infected bodily fluids, including blood, semen and vaginal fluids, making it both a sexually-transmitted infection and one that passes from mother-to-child, or via contaminated drug-injection equipment like needles.
Most healthy adults who contract the virus clear it on their own and develop lifelong immunity.

But when someone contracts hepatitis B as an infant or during childhood, it can become a chronic infection that causes long-term damage and inflammation to the liver, leading to serious complications or death.

items: All infants should be vaccinated against hep B, says Canadian vaccine advisory committee
Health Canada approves first "functional cure" for Chronic Hepatitis B

blocks.text: The burden of these infections is disproportionately carried by certain populations. There are higher rates among Indigenous communities, illicit drug users, individuals engaging in high-risk sexual activity and immigrants from countries where hepatitis B is more common.
Up until now, patients have required long-term antiviral therapy to surpress the virus, explained Dr. Curtis Cooper, who leads the Ottawa Hospital's viral hepatitis program.

"This new treatment, it completely clears all of the viral markers for hepatitis B out of the blood," he said, noting it offers "quite a bit of hope" for patients aiming to discontinue other treatments.
LISTEN | Health Canada approves first 'functional cure' for hepatitis B:
Ottawa Morning7:02Health Canada approves first "functional cure" for Chronic Hepatitis B
Drug may replace long-term antiviral treatment
The drug, called bepirovirsen, is a short-term course of injections which can lead to undetectable levels of virus DNA in some patients.

"From the data that we have now, if it works, then we can reassure [patients] that they have a functional cure and they won't need to take any further hepatitis B treatments in the future," said Coffin, from the University of Calgary.

The data is based on clinical trials comparing the drug to a placebo, which showed around one-fifth of patients still had the virus under control 24 weeks after stopping all other hepatitis B treatments, with undetectable levels in their blood.

items: Doctors, liver specialist team up to better fight hepatitis in Alberta
1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide is caused by infections, study suggests

blocks.text: The drug works only for a minority of patients, Coffin stressed, and "clinicians have to very carefully decide on which patients would be eligible and which would benefit from the treatment."

For instance, individuals with a history of cirrhosis — where healthy liver tissue is permanently scarred, blocking normal blood flow — don't qualify, Coffin noted. She added there can be more side effects from the shot, including a rash, compared to taking a daily anti-viral medication.

It's also not clear just how durable the treatment will be. Coffin says data is still emerging as more time passes since the clinical trials, with the latest figures showing the drug has a lasting impact of at least 96 weeks.
"Our expectation is that it will last," Coffin said. "But of course, we won't know that until we do the long-term follow-up in these patients."
CDC panel vote to stop hep B vaccine for babies called 'irresponsible'
Questions around cost, access

Dr. Eric Yoshida, a professor of medicine in the division of gastroenterology at the University of British Columbia, is skeptical of where the drug fits into the broader landscape for hepatitis B treatments.
While he agreed bepirovirsen offers a major scientific leap forward, he says access and cost could be barriers to uptake — meaning the drug may not reach many Canadians.

items: Trump signs executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations
New HIV infections in Canada are rising. Advocates say years of progress are at risk

blocks.text: In Japan, where the drug was approved earlier, Yoshida says a course of therapy costs roughly $84,000 Cdn. Though actual pricing for Canada isn't yet clear, he questioned whether private drug plans and the provinces will end up covering it.
"Looking into the future, well, this is the first generation. The next generation is probably going to be even better and even less expensive, so I think the future is looking bright," Yoshida said.
"But I think for the average Canadian patient with hepatitis B, it's probably not going to mean a heck of a lot."
N.W.T. dental patients possibly exposed to HIV and hepatitis want to see improved care
Canada calls for universal infant vaccination

Treatment possibilities aside, both Coffin and Yoshida stressed the need for more awareness of hepatitis B vaccination as a way to stamp out the virus for good. Yet global immunization programs for this virus remain fraught.

In November, Canada's vaccine advisors issued a new recommendation for all Canadian infants to receive the hepatitis B shot, which may — in time — align provinces that offer the shot at a mix of ages, from infancy to children in grades six or seven.
"If every country in the world vaccinated their newborns," said Yoshida, "I think hepatitis B would be basically on the way out."

But Canada's recent move is a stark contrast from the U.S., where the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) removed its longstanding universal hepatitis B vaccination recommendation for newborns in late 2025.

Many countries also struggle with hepatitis B immunization, leading to significantly higher rates of chronic infection in certain regions. In 2024, 75 per cent of all global hepatitis B-related deaths were across Africa and the Western Pacific, World Health Organization data shows.
"We still have a long way to go," Coffin said.

articles.title: With 1 candidate on the ballot, federal Green Party chooses its next leader
articles.summary: In any other party, Mike Morrice would be acclaimed as leader. But the Green Party of Canada prides itself on doing things differently than the political mainstream.

image.caption: Mike Morrice is seen at the launch of his Green Party leadership campaign in August. He's the sole candidate still in the race. (Kate Bueckert/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·New
In any other party, Mike Morrice would be acclaimed as leader. But the Green Party of Canada prides itself on doing things differently than the political mainstream.
Mike Morrice almost certain to be next Green leader
In any other party, Mike Morrice would be acclaimed. End of story.
But the Green Party of Canada prides itself on doing things differently than the political mainstream.
So it should come as no surprise that even though Morrice is the only leadership candidate on the ballot, Green Party members still get to have their say.
On Saturday evening, the federal Greens will announce their next leader. Party members vote using a ranked ballot, including the option none of the above.
"As someone running, it is important to me that I do have a mandate for members. And we'll see what that mandate looks like," Morrice said.

items: Former MP Mike Morrice only Green Party of Canada leadership candidate after Nira Dookeran withdraws

blocks.text: Noting participatory democracy is one of the founding values of the party, he suggested it would be difficult for the party not to proceed with the vote.
"I think it reflects on a political party that does lead with its values, which is what attracted me to the Greens in the first place," Morrice said.
2nd candidate dropped out
Outgoing leader Elizabeth May announced after the 2025 federal election that she would be stepping down, while staying on as the party's sole member of Parliament.
The search to find a new leader began officially in June. The second candidate in the race, Nira Dookeran of Ottawa, dropped out in September.
In a statement, Dookeran said she made the decision "for personal and family reasons" and "after much soul-searching."
Morrice was elected to Parliament in 2021. The one-term MP for the Ontario riding of Kitchener Centre lost his seat last year to a Conservative by a narrow margin of 358 votes.
Soon after the defeat, Morrice was named deputy leader of the party and declared the next Green candidate for Kitchener Centre.
Notably spending more time in places where the Greens are the strongest, Morrice said he has travelled to meet members across the country from Nanaimo, B.C., to Charlottetown.
"I've enjoyed having the chance to connect with Greens, to talk about both the challenges we faced as a party, but also get their ideas on the path forward," Morrice said.
Mike Morrice joins the race for party leadership

Éric Grenier, a polling analyst and publisher of The Writ, said if an election was called today Morrice would be a competitive candidate, along with May, the MP for Saanich-Gulf Islands for the last 15 years.
"But apart from that, the Greens aren't really in a strong position anywhere," Grenier said.
He called it a missed opportunity for Greens not to have a leadership race with other candidates.

"Certainly a contested race with some a number of quality candidates would have been a better outcome for everybody involved," Grenier said. "It's helpful for engaging members. It's helpful for raising money. It's helpful for getting media attention."
The Greens endured one of their worst defeats in the April 2025 election.
For the first time in 25 years, the party's national vote share dropped below two per cent. The party's co-leader, Jonathan Pedneault, failed to secure a seat and resigned.
May was first elected Green Party leader in 2006 and stepped down in 2019. May returned to lead the party in 2022, following the resignation Annamie Paul.
She said on Thursday that she plans to hand over leadership of the party this month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: PNP asks for proper public demonstrations ahead of ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Saturday asked the public to practice their right to assembly in a responsible manner ahead of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 4:34pm

Members of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the Philippine National Police enforce strict security measures on the roads inside the Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex leading to the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City on Saturday, November 16, 2026, where the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits are set to be held. DANNY PATA

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Saturday asked the public to practice their right to assembly in a responsible manner ahead of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits in Pasay City.
World leaders have started arriving in the Philippines on Saturday for the international conference amid continuing protest actions condemning the scheduled arrival of US President Donal Trump.

Students from multiple universities conducted nationwide walkouts on Friday to slam Trump's visit and the controversial US-led Pax Silica initiative. Transport group PISTON will stage a transport strike on Monday, also denouncing Trump.

"May karapatan ang bawat Pilipino na magsalita at magpahayag ng kanilang saloobin. We respect that. Ang hinihiling lang natin ay maging maayos ang ating pagkilos at sundin ang mga itinakdang lugar at proseso. We can protect the right to express ourselves while making sure that the safety of everyone is not put at risk," PNP Chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement.

(Every Filipino has the right to speak and express themselves. We respect that. We just ask that the actions be proper and to comply with the designated locations and process. We can protect the right to express ourselves while making sure that the safety of everyone is not put at risk.)

The PNP said that although it respects the people's right to assemble, heightened security arrangements are in place for the event. The police urged protesters to make use of "freedom parks," as the Public Assembly Act of 1985 also mandated the need for permits to hold public assemblies.
Nartatez has directed police personnel to maintain a professional, courteous, and measured approach when dealing with protestors.
The PNP urged organizers to coordinate with local government units and police authorities ahead of their activities.

The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits is set from November 16 to 18. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Timor-Leste Kay Rala Zanana Gusmao, and Brazilian President Lula da Silva are among the heads of state who have arrived for the summit. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sudan: Misery worsens amid plummeting aid for displaced people
articles.summary: Sudan's humanitarian crisis is exacerbated by cuts in international aid. Almost 34 million people are in need as war and drone strikes are making it difficult to deliver aid to the population.

image.caption: Sudanese civilians continue to suffer, but donor nations are cutting aid budgetsImage: Marwan Ali/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) are sounding the alarm: Serious funding gaps have depleted the supplies of emergency shelter and basic household goods intended for Sudan. Without urgent provision of flexible funding, even more families will have to cope without adequate protection from extreme weather conditions, insecurity, violence and exploitation in the coming months.

According to a recently published joint statement, $2.9 billion (€2.62bn) is needed for the United Nation's Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan. This funding is intended to provide life-saving aid to 20.4 million people in Sudan. So far, however, only 47% of the required funds have been raised.

A total of 33.7 million people in the war- and famine-stricken country are dependent on humanitarian aid. Some 15.4 million alone require emergency shelter and basic household items. However, due to a lack of funding, aid organizations have been able to assist only 10%.

More than three and a half years after the war began between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is still the site of the world's largest humanitarian and displacement crisis. About 8.6 million people fled within the country to escape the escalating violence and more than 4.6 million fled to neighboring countries. Another 5.2 million have returned to their regions of origin despite the ongoing war. However, their towns and infrastructure have been destroyed. Fighting, drone strikes and logistical problems further complicate the delivery of humanitarian aid.

Between 40,000 and 250,000 people have been killed. Accurate or updated figures are not available as fighting continues, satellite-based internet communication is curbed, and many aid organizations and observers have left the country.

blocks.caption: Sudan has been frequently described as the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crisisImage: Faiz Abubakr/Middle East Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Donors cut back on funding

"It's hard to imagine how people are supposed to survive," Marina Peter, chairwoman of the Sudan and South Sudan Forum in Germany, told DW. In large parts of the country, people have been cut off from humanitarian aid since the war began. Some have survived by eating roots. According to the Sudan expert, the fact that people are still returning to war zones from neighboring countries is also linked to shortages: Food rations have been drastically cut in refugee camps.

Ivo Körner, Sudan specialist at Caritas International, criticizes the international community for the sharp decline in aid. "Globally, we're seeing a dramatic drop in funding for humanitarian aid," Körner told DW. It's not just the United States that has slashed its contributions; Germany and the European Union are also providing significantly less funding than they did four or five years ago, he said.

In Sudan, Caritas International supports refugees and the communities hosting them with cash assistance, drinking water supplies, basic medical care and seeds. However, Sudan's Caritas' projects in 2026 have been financed exclusively through donations. While Körner hopes for additional funding from the German Foreign Office for Sudan projects, he predicts that funding opportunities will be significantly more limited than in previous years.

According to Sudan expert Marina Peters, the consequences of the crisis are becoming increasingly difficult to assess. "In many parts of the country, people have already been completely cut off from humanitarian aid since the start of the war," she told DW. Peter also notes that child mortality in Sudan is above average. However, it is nearly impossible to determine the actual extent of the crisis more precisely because the warring parties continue to obstruct humanitarian access.

blocks.caption: The Sudanese Armed Forces have been fighting for control of the entire country against the Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces for more than three yearsImage: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP

blocks.text: Who should take action?

On October 23, the United Kingdom and 31 other international partners, including Germany, issued a joint statement on the looming famine in Sudan. According to the statement, 19.5 million people — about 41% of the population — are suffering from acute food insecurity. The countries are calling on the warring parties to allow unimpeded access for humanitarian aid and to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure. At the same time, they are demanding an increase in international aid funding.

While Marina Peter welcomes the appeal in principle, she sees a contradiction. "The question is: Who is this appeal actually directed at?" Most of the signatories have themselves systematically cut funding for humanitarian aid and development cooperation. The appeal to the international donor community is thus ultimately directed at the states themselves.
Meanwhile, the Sudanese government based in the country's capital Khartoum — led by General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan's SAF — rejects all warnings of a famine.

In a statement dated October 26, it claims that the food situation in the country is reportedly reassuring and that government reserves and ongoing agricultural production are sufficient to meet demand. According to Khartoum, the warnings from Western countries amount to a politicization of the humanitarian situation.

Peter criticized this statement as "truly cynical and almost perfidious. The government's claim that humanitarian organizations have unrestricted access also does not reflect reality, she said. In many places, aid continues to be obstructed.

blocks.caption: Drone attacks on civilians have killed hundreds this yearImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: Drone attacks exacerbate dangers

In addition to hunger and displacement, the threat to civilians posed by the use of drones is also growing. The Peace for Sudan Platform issued an appeal on November 5 calling for an end to attacks on civilians, markets, hospitals, and water and electricity supplies. In the first three weeks of October alone, at least 306 people were killed in attacks. According to the UN Human Rights Office, drones claimed the lives of at least 1,120 civilians in the first half of 2026.

"Drone strikes are a major problem," Caritas' Körner confirmed. They cause widespread anxiety among the population and often strike civilians. Added to this is the danger to humanitarian workers. This makes local partner organizations all the more important, he said. They enjoy the trust of the local population, are deeply rooted in the regions and in some cases are able to reach areas that international aid workers can hardly access.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: How Camiguin intensified the yearner in me
articles.summary: One day is not enough to learn about the beauty of this volcanic island

blocks.text: Press play to hear the sounds of Camiguin
Story by Chau Morales • November 14, 2026
One day is not enough to learn about the beauty of this volcanic island.
Listen to this playlist while you read.

Clear, turquoise waters, clouds drifting over Mt. Hibok-Hibok and Mt. Vulcan, and a clownfish looking up as I swam above it – vivid scenes flash before me when I think of my recent trip to Camiguin, the “island born of fire.” Yet beyond these vivid memories, I was filled with questions, wondering what else I might have discovered had I stayed just a little longer.

I am still struck by a strange longing for places on the island I didn’t get to see. I searched up what I was feeling and found that there are a few words for it: Anemoia, a nostalgia for a time or place never lived through; and Sehnsucht, a German concept of aching yearning for a place or experience that feels out of reach.

The trip was a blur of plane rides, ferry runs, and long drives. Getting to and from Camiguin Island took up nearly half of our four-day stay, and with a full day dedicated to learning about the local government’s preservation efforts, we were left with one day to explore.
🎒 Field Guide
Explore more travel stories like this on Rappler’s Field Guide!
Explore More
What’s there

It was around 7 am on a Friday when we set foot on White Island. Although bare and straightforward, the C-shaped sandbar was captivating as it was wrapped in calm, impossibly vibrant turquoise waters. Despite the grey clouds that blanketed the skies, a cold, gentle breeze swept across the islet. Early as we were, the islet was already dotted with tourists.

Where most people hope for blue skies to capture the peaks of Mt. Hibok-Hibok and Mt. Vulcan in the backdrop, the gloomy September morning veiled them in soft clouds instead. Staring at those hidden peaks, I found myself hooked and caught in the mystery of what was out of sight.

As our boat docked on Mantigue Island, the wide stretch of beach opened up before us. It was only a short walk to the cottages, but every step made my eyes wander, basking in every detail of the beauty surrounding me.

Snorkeling was entirely new territory for me. Slipping on that mask was like unlocking an unseen world. One moment, I was just walking or sitting beneath the clear and shallow waters, but with the mask, I realized I was swimming alongside a vibrant school of small fish.
Cloudy by the minute we set foot
But the sun didn’t keep the island waiting too long

Yet, my newfound boldness had its limits. Further out, my new friends were calling for me to swim over and spot the sea turtles. But I didn’t trust my skills (or the lack of them) on open water just yet, so I stayed behind. Standing there, a quiet regret settled in. I knew at that moment that it became one of the reasons why I wish I would go back someday, hopefully, with enough summoned courage to explore further.

Seeking a different kind of comfort, we also wandered over to the island’s forest boardwalk. In seconds, you’re transported into a sanctuary. Shaded by trees, it was easy to forget we were surrounded by the ocean. It was a place to breathe in the island’s deep, undisturbed quiet. High in the trees, the birds chirped as they stayed hidden in the leaves. Much like the turtles out at sea, they hid their world out of sight.
Surrounded by a canopy of green as I take a stroll on the boardwalk
Immersed in lush greenery
The sun finally breaks through the trees
The other end of the boardwalk opens to another side of the island.

We ran through a series of iconic spots the rest of the day – from the freezing waters of Sto Nino Cold Spring and the rush of Tuasan Falls, to the lingering histories of the Old Church Ruins and Sunken Cemetery. We were moving fast, taking in as much of Camiguin as the night approached.
Leaving Mantigue, the sky was in a tug-of-war between grey clouds and bursts of sunlight.
A few sharp rocks couldn’t stop us from taking the plunge at Tuasan Falls.
Entrance to the ruins of the old Spanish church of Bonbon
Not haunting, but heavy with history.
The weight of its past lingers on the space.
Beneath the cross lies the Sunken Cemetery.
The entire Spanish burial ground was submerged when Mt. Vulcan erupted in 1871.

While the island’s landscapes and our speedrun of activities left my mind wishing we stayed longer, it’s the food that anchored me to the present. During our lunch in Mantigue, we tasted Surol, a comfortingly familiar soup like Tinola, but cooked with native chicken elevated by the aromatics of lemongrass and oregano. For a change, I did not take the usual rice route, but went with a boiled sweet potato. Outside the cold springs, we tried kiping, a massive cassava chip drizzled in rich, sweet latik sauce.

What really surprised me was Camiguin’s unexpected culinary range. At Txaleta de Camiguin, a single meal of gambas and callos set a new standard for my palate. The flavors and texture of the shrimp and beef tripe were striking and deeply memorable. These dishes made me realize that even if I left the island incomplete, I had another reason to long for my return.
An ode to the island in film
What wasn’t there

What makes Camiguin so captivating is how it protects its own rhythm. Even if it attracts travelers from across the world, the island remains blissfully unhurried. The locals haven’t fully adapted their lives to cater to rapid tourism. They still move at their own steady pace.

There are no corporate hotel giants dominating the coastline, only refined, quiet stays like Nouveau Resort. Nightlife isn’t a roaring scene yet; party and casual spots are confined to the Yumping area, but the place remains calm under the night sky.

The stillness is no accident; it is maintained. Through the local government’s VICE framework, Camiguin prioritizes people, nature, and responsible stewardship above commercialization. You’ll feel this stewardship everywhere: in the strict ban on single-use plastics, for example. I witnessed this firsthand during our lunch at Mantigue Island, where segregation was quietly enforced, down to collecting the soda bottles we used into designated bags.
What exists unseen

Because the afternoon spots were squeezed in together, the trip left me wanting more. I remember hoping to stick around longer and enjoy Tuasan Falls’ cold mountain water, and how every step on the barefoot walk across its riverbed sharpened my senses. I remember stepping into the deep waters of the Sto. Nino Cold Spring and nervously padding toward the edge, savoring even the fear. At the Old Church Ruins and Sunken Cemetery, I found myself holding back, wishing I had been given the quiet space to truly learn about the island’s past.

Most of all, the visit left me longing for a connection with the local life. When Camiguin Governor Xavier Jesus Romualdo spoke of local traditions where fishermen’s wives gather their husbands’ daily catch, host a community cookfest, and share meals with visitors, my heart sank a little knowing we missed the chance to witness these. I yearned to sit with the locals, and wished I could listen to their stories of how they defend and conserve their home in its purest form.

I realized that my yearning wasn’t just about missed photo ops, it was about depth. Getting to know a place is like meeting a new friend or a potential lover–it demands patience. It requires deep, quiet conversations with people who know its secrets, and the space to ask the right questions in return. On this trip, I was left mostly with lingering questions and the gentle ache of passing time.
Yet, for an emotional traveler, that longing isn’t defeat; it’s an invitation. If a place is meant to be part of your story, time will find a way to weave it back in.
The encounter was brief, but Camiguin moved slowly enough to leave a mark. Now I only wonder: what chapter of my life will bring me back? – Rappler.com

articles.title: ASEAN raises 2026 growth forecast to 4.7%
articles.summary: The ASEAN has raised its economic growth forecast for this year to 4.7% from 4.5%, although rising food and energy prices and tensions in the Middle East continue to threaten the region's outlook.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 4:15pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has raised its economic growth forecast for this year to 4.7% from 4.5%, although rising food and energy prices and tensions in the Middle East continue to threaten the region's outlook.
Trade Secretary Ma. Cristina Roque announced the revised forecast during the 39th ASEAN Coordinating Council meeting on Saturday, November 14, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

"Despite an increasingly challenging global environment, ASEAN's economic outlook remains relatively resilient," Roque said in remarks livestreamed on the Presidential Communications Office's official Facebook page.
The region's economy is expected to grow by 4.7% in 2027, she added.

Roque, however, said high food and energy prices, prolonged conflict in the Middle East, disruptions to energy markets and critical shipping routes, and the prospect of a strong El Niño continue to pose challenges to households, businesses and the agriculture sector.
On ASEAN's economic agenda, Roque said the bloc is on track to complete all 19 priority economic deliverables under the Philippines' chairship.
Fourteen are expected to be completed by the 49th ASEAN Summit, while the remaining five are targeted for completion by December.
The signing of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) is among the major developments under the Philippines' chairship.
Roque said the agreement would open opportunities for regional cooperation in digital transformation and economic development.
"Our task now is to ensure that they move beyond commitments and translate into practical support and opportunities for businesses, especially MSMEs and our people," she said.
Meanwhile, the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) Pillar has completed 87% of the activities under the AEC Blueprint 2025 as of November, equivalent to 3,379 activities, Roque said.
She said the bloc must complete the remaining activities and ensure that the blueprint's commitments benefit businesses, workers and communities.
Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, meanwhile, said ASEAN had maintained its unity despite geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty and other challenges confronting the region.
"ASEAN has shown that unity and solidarity are more than aspirations, they are the sources of our strategic capacity," Lazaro said.
She cited progress in maritime cooperation, economic integration, social protection and regional security during the Philippines' chairship.
Lazaro also said the region's security, economic growth and social resilience must be pursued together.
"ASEAN security, prosperity, and social resilience cannot be advanced in isolation," she said.
Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian, for his part, said the Philippines had pushed for a regional agenda focused on families, communities and inclusive development.
He cited initiatives on family resilience, youth leadership, digital innovation, environmental sustainability and food security.
"One important lesson from our chairship is that the quality of regional cooperation is ultimately reflected in the difference it makes in people's lives," Gatchalian said.
He said ASEAN's commitments must translate into policies and services that address the needs of communities, particularly those exposed to economic uncertainties and environmental risks.
"A more prosperous and secure ASEAN must also be one where people have the opportunity to participate, contribute, and live with dignity," he said.
The Philippines assumed the ASEAN chairship this year under the theme "Navigating Our Future, Together." Singapore will take over the chairmanship in 2027.

articles.title: Through buri weaving and filmmaking, Sampaloc, Quezon tells a new story
articles.summary: While the women of Sampaloc, Quezon keep the historic buri-weaving tradition alive, the town has also started building on its reputation as a film location to inspire local youth to explore careers…

items: Sampaloc, a town between Mauban and Lucban, is gaining attention as a filming destination, attracting artists like filmmaker Lav Diaz and providing economic benefits through film productions.
The Sine Sampaloc festival aims to develop local filmmaking talent and skills, although it has yet to feature films made by local filmmakers, focusing instead on creative activities for youth.
Alongside its growing film industry, Sampaloc's cultural heritage is preserved through traditional buri weaving, which remains an important part of the local economy and community identity.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Sandwiched between Mauban, the coastal gateway to Cagbalete Island, and Lucban, home of the Pahiyas Festival, the town of Sampaloc is easy to overlook. It remains under the radar while attracting artists such as filmmaker Lav Diaz, who has made the town his second home.

Sampaloc’s appeal is reflected in both its landscape and its people. During the three-month shoot in town for Lav Diaz’s Magellan, locals would spot Mexican lead star Gael Garcia Bernal low-key strolling around town, eating pancit at a neighborhood eatery, and blending in with the community.

The production of Magellan also brought economic benefits to the town. Empty-nesters opened unused bedrooms as homestays to accommodate cast and crew members, while dozens of locals found work as extras and additional film crew.

blocks.caption: Lav Diaz on Cannes-bound ‘Magellan,’ Gael Garcia Bernal, and how he ‘almost died’

blocks.text: Sampaloc has also served as a location for other productions, including the Netflix film Reroute, starring John Arcilla, Sid Lucero, and Cindy Miranda.

In the film, a car breakdown leaves Lucero and Miranda’s characters stranded, eventually leading them to the home of Arcilla’s character. Sampaloc’s landscape helps establish the film’s unsettling atmosphere, demonstrating the range of settings the town can offer filmmakers.

blocks.caption: The house of John Arcilla’s character in Netflix’s ‘Reroute.’ Photo by Marky Ramone Go

blocks.text: Alongside larger productions such as Magellan and smaller independent films shot in Sampaloc, the town hopes to build on its growing appeal as a filming destination.

Instead of just promoting its landscapes to filmmakers, it wants to encourage local youth to explore the different facets of filmmaking, from screenwriting, editing, and production design to acting, directing, and the technical work behind the camera.
Now in its second year, Sine Sampaloc has yet to produce a film made by local filmmakers. The municipality is still working to develop local interest and the skills needed to support film production.
For its second edition, the festival screened 10 selected short films that had won in previous editions of Cinemalaya and the Gawad CCP Para sa Alternatibong Pelikula.

None of the films was shot in Sampaloc or involved local filmmakers or actors. Instead, local participation took other creative forms: students choreographed interpretative dances inspired by each film, while aspiring production designers created tricycle floats representing the movies.

blocks.caption: The vast rice fields can serve as a beautiful backdrop to any film set outside the big city. Photo courtesy of Marboy Sayno

blocks.text: When asked about the inspiration behind Sine Sampaloc, Mayor Nikko Devanadera offered a practical answer. The goal, he explained, is to attract film productions to the town and encourage them to spend locally, while developing a pool of homegrown talent that can support the industry.
“One is to invite film productions and make them spend here. It’s really economic because the youth development aspect is actually skills development, skills pipeline for the productions,” he said.

For Devanadera, the festival’s creative activities serve a practical purpose: preparing young people for opportunities in film production while equipping them with skills they can use in other fields.

The municipality also hopes to expand these opportunities through workshops and equipment for creative work, including video editing and post-production. These skills could open doors beyond film, including in graphic design and visual arts.
High school students who attended the workshops also spent an afternoon with filmmaker Zig Dulay, known for directing Green Bones, who introduced them to the basics of screenwriting.
But filmmaking is not the only creative pursuit Sampaloc hopes to develop.
Somewhere in town, a group of women continues a traditional livelihood that once helped send generations of children to school.
Buri weaving may not attract film production companies, but it remains an important part of Sampaloc’s cultural and economic history.

“During my teens in the ’70s, almost all the kids here in Sampaloc were sent to school through the buri weaving of our parents,” said Hermilina “Aling Tessy” Diaz, 65, who has been weaving buri for almost 50 years.
Today, only a few dozen buri, also called buli, weavers remain in Sampaloc, a far cry from Aling Tessy’s younger years.

“All those kids, of course, grew up to become professionals. Others worked abroad, while others took up different jobs,” she said, explaining how the craft gradually lost its foothold in the local economy.
But buri, Aling Tessy points out, remains part of Sampaloc’s culture.

blocks.caption: A weaver prepares strips of buri palm leaves. Photo by Marky Ramone Go

blocks.text: Buri comes from the leaves of the buri palm, one of the Philippines’ native palms. Its leaves are prized for their strength and versatility and have long been used to make baskets, bags, fans, hats, boxes, and other household items.
In Sampaloc, the remaining weavers have organized themselves as KUMARI Weavers, or “Kababaihang Umaaksyon para sa Maunlad at Responsableng Kababaihang may Integridad.”

The weaving, or paglala, is only one part of the work. Before a single leaf can be woven, the raw buri has to go through a painstaking process: harvesting, stripping, sun-drying, boiling, drying again, flattening, and preparing the strips for weaving. Only then does the actual paglala begin.
Many of the finished bags and baskets sell for only P200 to P400. The obvious question is why they cost so little, considering the time, skill, and labor that go into making each piece.

For buyers, it is worth remembering that bargaining down the price of a handcrafted item can come at the expense of the very artisans whose work deserves support. These women have spent years perfecting their craft. Their work deserves a price that justifies the time and skill involved, not just the cost of materials.

As Sampaloc explores opportunities in filmmaking and other creative industries, its buri weavers remain part of the town’s cultural and economic life. Both represent skills and talent worth investing in.
For KUMARI Weavers, keeping the craft alive means making it a steady source of income and giving younger generations a reason to learn it.
Whether through films or traditional crafts, Sampaloc has a lot of stories and skills to build on. – Rappler.com
