articles.title: Nigeria: How the pcoming elections are influeced by the rise of AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their…

image.caption: Nigeria's 2027 elections take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformationImage: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nigeria has just over two months to go to the polls, with incumbent President Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images, and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general elections; instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI-use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming elections could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and indeed the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria finds itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online; in the run up to the 2023 elections, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates, or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

blocks.caption: Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be manipulated easily to believe AI-driven fake newsImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial Intelligence: Various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI generated fakes are possible," says Akintunde Babatunde, Executive Director of the Abuja-based Center for Journalism, Innovation and Development (CJID)."

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Have some elections become an empty ritual?
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development (CDD-West Africa), meanwhile told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into INEC's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added however that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity, but that the real threat rather lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," Mgbeahuruike said.

blocks.caption: Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologiesImage: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Director-General of Voice of Nigeria (VON), Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech in elections
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a new system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition; however, during the 2023 general elections, this voting process was marred by system failures of BVAS, as poor cell signal delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

blocks.caption: In Nigeria, voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP

blocks.text: However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy:

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth; the 2023 elections recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27 percent of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.title: Espionage accusations: a pressure tactic for Turkish government critics
articles.summary: This week's arrest of an employee of a German foundation in Istanbul has put focus back on the Erdogan administration's pressure tactics. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

image.caption: Yonca Verdioglu Sik (right) after her release with her husband, journalist and MP Ahmet Sik (left)Image: ANKA

blocks.text: When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of the German organization, the Heinrich Böll Foundation, for whom Verdioglu Sik works. For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and women's, minority and LGBTQ+ rights.
During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now subject to a travel ban too.
Pressure on politicians

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released. Nonetheless her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. Sik is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the current government's harshest critics.

Recently Sik has been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefitted members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and their associates.
Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.
"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been levelled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like non-governmental organizations and foundations.
Diplomatic disputes

Such accusations were often followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. What the many instances have in common though is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.
In the past such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

For example in 2015, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.
In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

blocks.caption: Journalist Deniz Yücel was labeled a "German agent" by Turkey's presidentImage: Bernd Elmenthaler/IMAGO IMAGES

blocks.text: Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.
Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.
'Hostage diplomacy'
Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, notes that the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argues. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.
"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.
LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."
These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas observes.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," Tas explains. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.
It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas says.

blocks.caption: US pastor Andrew Brunson (center, white shirt) with his wife after his release in 2018Image: Getty Images/AFP/B. Kilic

blocks.text: Punishing process

The case of US cleric Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already standing trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.
In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage.
The Kavala case demonstrates this. He was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.
But Tas says that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."
This story was originally published in German.
No future in Turkey?

articles.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
articles.summary:
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars

Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be…

blocks.text: Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais.

In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.

Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.

blocks.caption: New airport style drive-in biometrics kiosks at Eurotunnel in Calais. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.

In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.

The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France, have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.

blocks.caption: The new drive-in fingerprinting terminals at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.

Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.

Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.

Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.

blocks.caption: The new drive-in border controls at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.

Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

November 14, 2026
Delhi overtakes Lahore as world's most polluted city
On Friday, Delhi's Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 334, categorized as "hazardous"making it the most polluted major city globally, according to Swiss air quality monitoring group IQAir.
The Indian capital's AQI was recorded to be higher than Lahore in Pakistan on Friday, which made it the most polluted city globally.

India's official Central Pollution ​Control Board, however, recorded the AQI higher at 403 and ‌rated ⁠it "severe."
The difference between the Indian and Swiss readings is caused by the fact that the two use different AQI scales and methodologies to calculate and categorize air pollution ​levels.
India's worst air pollution crisis isn't in its megacities
Visibility in Delhi is significantly impacted as a thick layer of smog has enveloped the city.
In many parts of northern India and Pakistan, pollution poses a seasonal problem as the ​cold, heavy air of ​winter traps vehicle emissions, construction dust and smoke from agricultural ​burning.

articles.title: Trump, other Quad leaders to meet in Manila on Tuesday, sources say
articles.summary: Leaders of the US, Japan, Australia and India are expected to meet on Tuesday on the sidelines of a key Asian meeting in Manila, two people familiar with the planning said, marking the first summit…

blocks.text: Published November 14, 2026 2:22pm

Leaders of the US, Japan, Australia and India are expected to meet on Tuesday on the sidelines of a key Asian meeting in Manila, two people familiar with the planning said, marking the first summit of the "Quad" nations in two years.

The Quad group of Indo-Pacific powers is widely considered a counterweight to China's growing influence in the region, although its members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated last month that the Quad leaders could meet on the sidelines of the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which begins on Sunday in the Philippine capital.
The supply of critical minerals is expected to be on the Quad summit agenda, one of the people said.

"The leaders are likely to take up the issue of free and unimpeded commercial shipping lanes in order to secure energy supplies from across the world," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he is not authorized to speak with the media. "The issue of attacks on commercial ships is very likely to be taken up."

The second person, from the Philippine government and briefed on the preparations, said the Quad leaders were expected to gather shortly after US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila on Tuesday, the last day of the ASEAN summit.
The Manila gathering would be the first Quad leaders' meeting since Trump returned to office last year.
Quad leaders last met in September 2024 in Delaware, reaffirming their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific and announcing initiatives to strengthen maritime security cooperation. —Reuters

articles.title: Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?
articles.summary: Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the…

image.caption: 'It's giving anxiety about the future,' reads the sign at a Gen Z protest in Hamburg Image: Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.
Pensions and poverty among the elderly

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.
By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.
What Germans young and old think about the pension system
Rent and housing costs

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.
This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.
Investment in education

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.
Climate change

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."
This article was originally published in German.

House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin on Saturday said discussions on the possible replacement for Sara Duterte as the country's vice president are too early to be held amid her ongoing impeachment trial.
"For me, it's very premature to talk about who the next Vice President will be," Garin said at a news forum in Quzon City.
"It's not yet the time to talk about that kasi dapat tignan muna 'yung impeachment. Hindi naman natin sinasabi na talagang mai-impeach na si vice president," she said.
(It's not yet the time to talk about that because the focus should be on the impeachment trial. We cannot say for sure that she will be convicted.)
"Itong lahat ay depende sa senator-judges at depende sa kampo niya kung masasagot ang mga katanungan," she added.
(This all depends on the senator-judges, and her camp if they will be able to answer the questions raised.)
Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro earlier said President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. has not discussed or considered a replacement for the vice president.
Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano earlier urged fellow senators to decline any potential offers for the vice presidency should Duterte be convicted.
Senator Francis "Chiz" Escudero previously declared he would refuse the post due to a conflict of interest as a senator-judge.
Under the 1987 Constitution, if the vice presidency becomes vacant, the President nominates a new Vice President who must then be confirmed by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress.
"Just in case mayroon nang annointed then we cross the bridge when it comes," Garin said.

Duterte's spokesperson Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. earlier said the focus should be on questions involving the fairness of the Senate impeachment court, the constitutionality of the conviction threshold, and alleged due process violations. He likewise said it was premature to discuss about replacements for the vice president. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
articles.summary: Trump will discuss the "reduction of nuclear weapons" during the unprecedented talks, a spokeswoman says.

blocks.text: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.

But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.

Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its biggest trade partner.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Russian state news agency Tass reported that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had said there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

articles.title: Philippines, Canada conclude free trade deal talks, eye 2027 signing
articles.summary: The Philippines and Canada have concluded negotiations for a free trade agreement (FTA), with both countries eyeing its signing in 2027, Malacañang said Saturday, November 14.

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 1:44pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shake hands during their meeting on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits on Nov. 14, 2026.
Presidential Communications Office via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and Canada have concluded negotiations for a free trade agreement (FTA), with both countries eyeing its signing in 2027, Malacañang said Saturday, November 14.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met on Saturday on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, where they discussed the trade deal and other areas of cooperation.
The proposed agreement covers trade in goods and services, investments, digital trade and small and medium-sized enterprises.

In a statement posted on Facebook, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said the FTA could help Philippine businesses expand their reach in the Canadian market and create more income opportunities for local entrepreneurs and workers.
The agreement could also benefit Filipinos providing services online through provisions covering digital trade.
Marcos and Carney also discussed investment opportunities under the Luzon Economic Corridor, particularly in transportation, infrastructure, agri-food, food logistics and cold-chain technologies.
The two leaders likewise reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening defense, security and maritime cooperation, as well as promoting peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region.
The conclusion of negotiations follows the two leaders' meeting during Marcos' official visit to Canada in July, when they committed to completing discussions on the FTA within the year.
Both governments are now working toward signing the agreement in 2027, the PCO said.

articles.title: Prosecution sees no need for more evidence in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel does not see the need to present more evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte in her ongoing impeachment trial.

blocks.text: AMID DOLLAR ACCOUNTS
Published November 14, 2026 1:23pm
The House prosecution panel does not see the need to present more evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Vice President Sara Duterte in her ongoing impeachment trial.

At a news forum in Quezon City, House private prosecutor Benjamin "Jay" Tolosa Jr. said the panel is satisfied with the pieces of evidence it presented already on the supposed unexplained wealth and undeclared assets amounting to P817.87 million held by Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio.
“We’re satisfied with that. We don’t see the need to present additional evidence,” Tolosa said.
This came amid reports that the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) informed the Senate impeachment court that the Vice President held dollar accounts in the bank.
Duterte’s defense team, however, decided not to present a witness from the BPI.
Nonetheless, Tolosa said the prosecution was ready to cross examine the witness from BPI concerning the alleged dollar accounts of the Vice President.

“All other foreign currency denominated accounts hindi po ‘yan na-subpoena dahil nga hindi ‘yan pinayagan dahil sa applicable bank secrecy laws. So, we’re just mentioning na napansin namin na itong inatras na testigo may naka-mention na sa mga dokumento pertaining to foreign currency, dollar accounts ng Vice President,” he said.

(All other foreign currency denominated accounts were not subpoenaed because it is not allowed under applicable bank secrecy laws. So we're just mentioning that we noticed that this witness which was withdrawn was mentioned in documents pertaining to foreign currency, dollar accounts of the Vice President.)

The lawyer noted that the prosecution team is confident on the pieces of evidence, such as records of foreign currency transactions of Calle88, which is 47.5% owned by Carpio, it has already presented during the trial.
Meanwhile, the defense panel of the Vice President is likely to finish presenting its case before the end of November.
The next proceedings for Duterte’s impeachment trial are scheduled for November 19 to 20, after which the Senate will take a break from the trial to focus on the 2027 national budget.
Thereafter, the next trial day is expected to resume on December 1. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government
articles.summary:
Prospect of partial return to Budapest by Central European University suggests confidence in Hungary’s future

A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to…

blocks.text: A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.

Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.

So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.

The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.

The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.

The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.

blocks.caption: CEU’s main building in Budapest, pictured in 2018. Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/Reuters

blocks.text: Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.
“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”

But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.
Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.

According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.

The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”

When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.
after newsletter promotion
He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.
Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.

“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”

Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.

The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”

articles.title: Senegal Youth Olympics in Dakar end on high note
articles.summary: Enthusiastic crowds attended the games in Senegal, with China taking home the most gold medals. It's the first Olympic Games since Russia's war on Ukraine where Russian athletes can compete under…

image.caption: The Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar was held from October 31 to November 13 Image: Sylvain Cherkaoui/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Senegal Summer Youth Olympics in Dakar ended Friday after two weeks of games on a high note.

It's the first time an African country has hosted an Olympic event, and African nations also brought home a record haul of medals. The Games were met with enthusiasm, with Dakar's streets and beaches filled with sports fans.
Nearly 2,700 young athletes took part in the games, which featured 153 medal events across 25 sports.
IOC president on Senegal games: 'Expectations have been exceeded'

"There is a beautiful African proverb, 'It take a village to raise a child.' And if these Youth Olympic Games have shown us anything it is what can happen when an entire country comes together for its young people," International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said in a thank-you ceremony on Friday.

Coventry praised the Senegalese people for hosting the games: "You have shown the world what Senegal and Africa are capable of, and when people come together behind a shared dream, how strong that can make us. You have every reason to be so proud."
She said earlier in the week that "expectations have been exceeded" when it came to Senegal hosting the games and that it shows what African nations are capable of in the future.
Which countries took home the most medals?
China took home the most gold medals at 18.

Japan took home 11 gold medals, whereas Russia received eight. It was the first time Russian athletes took part in an Olympic event under their own national flag since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.
Egypt won six gold medals, and Ethiopia and Senegal each earned five.

blocks.caption: Female wrestler Elisabeth Diatta, who is 16 years old, took home Senegal's first gold medalImage: Kadir Caliskan/United World Wrestling/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was the first time Senegal had ever won an Olympic gold, with 136 Senegalese athletes participating in the games.
The next Summer Youth Olympics will take place in 2030, with Chile, Paraguay and Thailand having confirmed their bids to host the games.

articles.title: Trump to meet Xi, Putin for three-way huddle on nuclear arms talks
articles.summary: The White House has said President Donald Trump will urge Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin to discuss cutting nuclear arsenals in Shenzhen next week, though a senior US official expects no agreement.

image.caption: The meeting would be the first of its kind if it happens as scheduled Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: United States President Donald Trump will push for nuclear arms reductions when he meets Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next week, the White House said Friday.
A senior US official said no agreement is expected, Reuters reported.
What do we know?
The meeting is set for Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen and would be the first of its kind.

"He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters. Trump will also raise the US-Israeli war against Iran but is not expected to bring up Ukraine, the official told Reuters.

"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said. "This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things."
Where does China stand?
China has long resisted nuclear talks with Washington, arguing that Russia and the US, which hold larger arsenals, should speak directly.
In October, its Foreign Ministry said it would be "neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage."
Chinese state media have said Xi will hold "bilateral" talks at the summit but have not mentioned a trilateral meeting. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment on the White House announcement.

The US-Russia New START treaty expired in February, leaving the world’s biggest arsenals without major limits. Russia has the most stored warheads, followed by the US and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Trump leaves Monday for a four-day Asia trip that includes a stop in the Philippines.

articles.title: What we know about the longest ground stop since 9/11
articles.summary: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack or a Microsoft outage.

blocks.text: US ground stop caused by 'incredibly old air traffic control system', Duffy says
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.
'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.
Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.
"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.
American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport
What caused the ground stop?
Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.
"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.
He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.
"It's going to continue to fail," he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.
He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.
Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.
Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

articles.title: PAL monitors US flight situation after nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Flag carrier Philippine Airlines is monitoring its flights to and from the United States after the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel…

blocks.text: November 14, 2026 | 11:11am
Passengers watch departure flights screens at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026.
AFP / Kamil Krzaczynski

MANILA, Philippines — Flag carrier Philippine Airlines is monitoring its flights to and from the United States after the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel for several hours on Friday.
In an advisory on Saturday, PAL said it continues to monitor its US flights as operations normalize.
"Passengers are advised to check their flight status through PAL’s official communication channels for the latest updates," the airlines said.
The FAA imposed the nationwide ground stop following a communications outage that US officials attributed to the country's aging air traffic control system.
The disruption left hundreds of thousands of passengers stranded, with some travelers forced to disembark from planes shortly before departure.
Nearly 6,000 flights were canceled, including some international routes, according to flight tracking service FlightAware.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the outage on outdated equipment, including switches, routers and copper telephone lines used by the country's air traffic control system.
Duffy described the incident as a legacy system problem and renewed his call for Congress to fund the modernization of the US air traffic control system.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said there was no evidence that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or an artificial intelligence-related attack.
The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop after about four hours. However, flight disruptions were expected to continue as airlines worked to address delays and cancellations caused by the outage.

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starship rocket, fails to recover booster
articles.summary: SpaceX had planned to catch and reuse both stages of its biggest rocket for the first time. But the booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico, while the spacecraft continued into orbit.

image.caption: Fingers crossed that Saturday's landing of the top part of the rocket won't end like the boosterImage: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP

blocks.text: US company SpaceX has successfully launched the latest flight of its Starship spacecraft into orbit but did not recover the booster rocket as planned.
The company, owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk, is hoping to develop a fully reusable rocket system. It had planned to recover both the booster and the upper stage, which is the spacecraft itself.
Instead of landing back at the launch site, the booster exploded above the Gulf of Mexico. The upper stage is currently in orbitand the plan is to recover it on Saturday when it returns to Earth.
It is to be caught by mechanical arms upon landing back at the launch pad, marking the first time the spacecraft would return to Earth. It could then potentially be reused in the future.
In addition to testing the reusable rocket system, the mission also delivered 26 of SpaceX’s satellitesfor its Starlink network.
How did the launch go?

SpaceX's Starship is the world's largest and most powerful rocket system. At 124 meters (407 feet) tall, it consists of a spacecraft mounted on a booster rocket. Both stages were designed from the outset to be fully reusable.

At the launch, both the spacecraft and booster successfully lifted off from the SpaceX South Texas Starbase site. While the Friday launch was an uncrewed mission, Starship is designed to carry both crew and cargo.

blocks.caption: Both booster and Starship at the launch of the missionImage: Steve Nesius/REUTERS

blocks.text: On its return path, the booster diverted from its flight path to the launch site and steered to a designated area over the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded over the sea surface. The reasons for the failure of the controlled landing were not immediately clear.
"Not sure right now why we weren't able to bring it back," SpaceX's Dan Huot said.
The upper stage continued into orbit and soon after began releasing the 26 satellites it was carrying.
It is scheduled to return to Earth on Saturday.
Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.

In previous launches, the Starship booster was successfully recovered. The upper stages of the 14 previous Starship missions have all ended up in the ocean though, either by design or because of failures.
The new objective of Friday’s launch was to recover both stages of the Starship launch system.
Currently, SpaceX is mostly using smaller Falcon rockets, which are not fully reusable because the second stage cannot be recovered.
Musk said he expected SpaceX to conduct Starship launches once a week by early 2027.
The project has received billions of dollars in NASA funding, with SpaceX also investing at least $15 billion.
The main goal of the program is to put astronauts on the Moon by 2028 although outstanding technical challenges could delay that schedule.

articles.title: US lifts nationwide ground stop for airports hours after halting all departures
articles.summary: The US federal aviation regulator has lifted a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Trump administration officials blame "overloaded" and "outdated" systems for the hourslong halt to departures.

image.caption: Flights were delayed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, which serves the nation's capital Image: Jonathan Ernst/REUTERS

blocks.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) canceled a ground stop on all national flights hours after stopping departures at US airports on Friday.
"We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s old copper lines. We use an old system," US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. "It was a legacy network problem."

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the communications breakdown resulted from a cyberattack or artificial intelligence and that the ⁠public ​was ​never ​in danger.

Over 4,500 flights were canceled Friday and about 700 for Saturday and over 10,000 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, according to the FlightAware aviation tracker. With some 11,000 flights scheduled to depart from US airports after 4 p.m. local time (2200 UTC), more cancellations were expected, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.
What do we know so far?
"All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA had said earlier Friday.

The agency said the ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis."
The agency said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution."
In a post on X, Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
"FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote.

The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation, Eurocontrol, said all flights departing for US airports from its 42 member states were suspended following a request from the FAA to deal with technical issues.
Canada implementing 'traffic management' measures at major airports

Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes."
"Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.
Toronto Pearson Airport said flights between Toronto and the US have been impacted by the ground stop.
The FAA ground stop order came a day after Duffy asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers.
It's the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.

articles.title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
articles.summary:
The former coalminer’s claim Australians are being ‘demographically replaced’ sparked wide criticism, but his party has shown no signs of dumping him

  • Get our

blocks.text: In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation leader upper house candidate Stuart Bonds launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by non-white immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the GOAT, an acronym for the greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.
Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”
“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.
The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.
But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.
“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.
One Nation could ‘clean the deck’ in regions
The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.
“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.
“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”
after newsletter promotion

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.
And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.
Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.
“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”
The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.
“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.
The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.
But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preferences flows aren’t guaranteed.
But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.
“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.
“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”

articles.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global disruption that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
articles.summary:
Experts say outage exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.
Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.
“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.
Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.
“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.
The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.
“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.
Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.
Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.
after newsletter promotion
Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.
Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.
In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”
